question: What are two advantages of using an Agile project management tool? Choose 2 answers
optionA: Consolidate project artifacts to a common repository.
optionB: Better relationships with business stakeholders.
optionC: Improve governance with gate steps in development.
optionD: Increased visibility into sprint and project status.
explanation:
Both keyed advantages are about where information lives. An Agile tool consolidates the project's artefacts - stories, acceptance criteria, decisions, links to the change that implemented each one - into one place the whole team reads, instead of a scatter of documents and message threads. And it makes status continuously visible: the board shows what is in progress and what is blocked, and the sprint reports show whether the work will land, without anyone assembling a status update by hand.
The rejected options are outcomes rather than features. Better stakeholder relationships may follow from the visibility, but no tool delivers them. Gate-based governance is a process a business chooses to impose; a tool can record the gates but does not supply the authority behind them.

https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management

question: What are two roles a project Steering Committee plays in determining what methodologies are used? Choose 2 answers
optionA: Designing a methodology that will meet a particular project's requirements.
optionB: Approving deviations from the chosen methodology, when required to address project issues.
optionC: Enforcing that corporate project stage gates are part of the chosen methodology.
optionD: Setting the criteria for selecting Agile or Waterfall methodology to be used on internal projects.
explanation:
A steering committee governs; it does not deliver. Its two roles here are both decisions about policy rather than practice: setting the criteria by which any given project is judged suitable for Agile or for Waterfall, and then approving the departures from that policy when a particular project needs one. Both are exception-and-standard decisions that need authority above any single project.
Designing a methodology is specialist work that a delivery or PMO function does, and enforcing that corporate stage gates appear in the process is an assurance activity carried out on each project, not a committee decision.
Note that this item is governance practice rather than a Salesforce platform fact - no vendor documentation settles who sits on a steering committee. The references below describe the surrounding release governance and are orienting rather than decisive.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.deploy_best_practices.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: At Universal Containers, Salesforce administrators are making changes to permission sets under instruction from the business. Randomly, various SOQL statements are failing. What strategy could be advised to bring this issue to the developer's attention earlier?
optionA: Ask administrators to only make changes to profiles instead.
optionB: Create a sandbox refresh strategy to ensure each sandbox is refreshed every day.
optionC: Extract each permission set, commit and merge to source control, and run through CI checks.
optionD: Advise developers to switch to SOSL queries that are more robust instead.
explanation:
The failures are random because nobody can see the change that caused them. Permission sets are metadata, so the fix is to stop treating them as untracked admin clicks: retrieve them into the repository, commit them like any other change, and let continuous integration run the test suite against the result. Salesforce makes the same argument for the org development model - "a source repo can help to mitigate the pain point of keeping environments in sync. By externalizing the changes for each release, the team knows that the source repo reflects what they are delivering" - and a build that fails on the commit tells the developer which permission change broke which query, at the moment it happened.
The alternatives address something else. Profiles have the same invisibility problem as permission sets, so switching between them changes nothing. SOSL is a different search language, not a defence against a field the running user can no longer see. And daily refreshes across every sandbox would destroy in-flight work to fix a visibility problem that source control solves.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/org-development-model/plan-for-changes-to-your-org2
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) has used Salesforce for the last 6 years with 50% custom code. UC has recently implemented continuous integration. UC wants to improve old test classes whenever new functionality invalidates tests. UC also wants to reduce the deployment time required. What should the architect recommend?
optionA: Do not execute any test classes in sandboxes and Production.
optionB: Execute all test classes in sandboxes and selected test classes in Production.
optionC: Do not execute test classes in sandboxes and all test classes in Production.
optionD: Test classes cannot be executed in sandboxes.
explanation:
The two goals pull in opposite directions, so they get different answers in different places. In the CI sandboxes, run everything: RunLocalTests executes "all tests in your org... except the ones that originate from installed managed and unlocked packages", which is what surfaces the old test classes that new functionality has invalidated - the stated goal of improving them. Time there costs nothing a user notices.
Production is where the clock matters, so narrow the set: RunSpecifiedTests means "only the tests that you specify in the runTests option are run", which trims the deployment window to the tests that cover what is being deployed. Note the granularity - runTests takes class names, one per entry, not individual methods.
The remaining options either skip testing in production, which the platform does not allow for a production deployment, or claim sandboxes cannot run tests at all.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_deploy.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm

question: Universal Containers has five development teams. The performance of the teams has been good, but the number of bugs has been increasing. After each sprint, they need more time to understand the code and make changes. What are two ways to improve the performance? Choose 2 answers
optionA: Sprint review process.
optionB: Define a team that will analyze/approve all changes.
optionC: Define and follow code standards.
optionD: Version control system to identify who is generating the bugs.
explanation:
The symptom names the cause: the teams need more time to understand the code after each sprint, which is a readability and consistency problem rather than a skill problem. Shared, enforced code standards are what make five teams' output legible to each other - naming, structure, error handling and trigger patterns that a reader can predict. The sprint review is the recurring point where the rising defect count becomes visible as a trend and the team can change how it works, rather than absorbing it sprint after sprint.
A central board approving every change converts a quality problem into a queue, and it removes the incentive for teams to own quality themselves. Using version history to identify who produced a bug is available in any repository, but attribution does not reduce defects and it discourages the honest reporting that does.
Note that this item is a team-process judgment rather than a platform fact - no Salesforce documentation settles it. The reference below is the closest official guidance on governance and change-management practice, and is orienting rather than decisive.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.deploy_best_practices.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers is a global organization that maintains regional production instances of Salesforce. One region has created a new application to track shipping containers. The CIO has requested that this new application be used globally by all the Salesforce instances and further maintained and modified regionally by local administrators. Which two deployment tools will support the request? Choose 2 answers
optionA: Ant Migration Tool
optionB: Developer Console
optionC: VS Code with Salesforce Extension
optionD: Change Sets
explanation:
Change sets cannot leave the family they belong to. They travel over a deployment connection, and "a deployment connection alone doesn't enable change sets to be sent between orgs" - each org must additionally be authorized to send and receive. Those connections exist between a production org and its own sandboxes, not between one region's production org and another's, so a change set cannot carry this app across independent regional instances.
Metadata API tooling has no such boundary. Both the Ant Migration Tool and the Salesforce Extensions for VS Code authenticate to whichever org you point them at and deploy the same retrieved component set into each one, which is what shipping a single app to every regional production org requires. The Developer Console edits one org in place and deploys nothing.
Currency note: Salesforce retired the Ant Migration Tool in Spring '24. It still runs, but receives no new functionality beyond API v59.0, and the Salesforce CLI is now the supported command-line route to the same Metadata API.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.changesets_about_connection.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/file_based.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/2024/01/moving-on-from-the-ant-migration-tool-to-sf-cli-v2

question: Universal Containers has just completed several projects, including new custom objects and custom fields. Administrators are having difficulty maintaining the application due to not knowing how objects and fields are being used. Which two options should an architect recommend? Choose 2 answers
optionA: Create design standards to consistently use the description field on custom objects.
optionB: Create design standards with a document to store all custom objects and custom fields.
optionC: Create design standards to consistently use the description field on custom fields.
optionD: Create design standards to require help text on all custom fields and custom objects.
optionE: Create design standards to require all custom fields on all custom object page layouts.
explanation:
The distinction that decides this is who each field is for. On a custom field, description is "description of the field" - documentation aimed at whoever maintains the org - while inlineHelpText "represents the content of field-level help", which renders next to the input for the end user. An admin trying to work out whether a field is still in use needs the first, and putting maintenance notes in the second shows them to every user filling in the form.
The practical advantage is that both descriptions are field metadata: they are retrieved, deployed and version-controlled with the component itself, so the documentation cannot drift away from what it documents. A separate register of objects and fields is accurate only until the next change nobody records, which is the situation the admins are already in.
Requiring every custom field on every page layout is a different matter entirely and would make the problem worse, not better.

question: Universal Containers is adopting Scrum as an Agile methodology and wants to choose a software tool to support the adoption. What three key features of an Agile development support tool should an architect look for? Choose 3 answers
optionA: Work (for example, user stories or tasks) assignment.
optionB: Email notifications when work is created or changed.
optionC: Sprint backlog management.
optionD: Product backlog prioritization.
explanation:
The question is specifically about supporting Scrum, so the features to look for are the ones Scrum's artefacts require. A prioritized product backlog is the ordered list everything else is drawn from. A sprint backlog holds what the team has committed to for the current sprint, pulled from that product backlog. And work items have to be assignable, because a sprint is executed by named people picking up specific stories.
A Kanban board is a genuinely useful feature and the reason it is the odd one out is framework rather than quality - it belongs to Kanban, where "the workflow is mapped into columns" and work is pulled continuously rather than committed sprint by sprint. Email notification on change is a generic capability of nearly any tracker and tells you nothing about whether the tool supports Scrum.

https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/scrum-and-kanban-at-salesforce/learn-about-scrum

question: Universal Containers (UC) is considering implementing a minor change policy for a series of low-risk user stories that are commonly received by the UC admins. The policy would allow admins to make these changes directly in production. UC does not have continuous integration/continuous delivery (CI/CD) in place. Which three best practices should the architect suggest UC follow for their new change policy? Choose 3 answers
optionA: Downstream environments will not be automatically updated when production changes.
optionB: Minor changes do not need to be documented and can be made at any time.
optionC: Minor changes should be thoroughly documented and follow some type of standard cadence.
optionD: All changes should still be tested.
optionE: CI/CD is required to successfully manage minor changes.
explanation:
A minor-change policy is a decision to accept some risk, not to abandon control, so the three practices that matter are the ones that keep the change visible and reversible. Every change still gets tested, because low risk is an estimate rather than a guarantee. Every change is documented and made on a predictable cadence, so the org's current state can be reconstructed later and two admins do not edit the same thing on the same afternoon.
The third is the consequence nobody plans for: changes made directly in production do not flow backwards. Downstream sandboxes keep the state they were refreshed with, so the next release from a sandbox can overwrite a production-only change unless it has been reapplied there. Refreshing is what closes that gap, and a Full sandbox can only take that refresh every 29 days.
The two rejected options are the extremes - that minor changes need no documentation at all, and that a change policy is impossible without CI/CD. Neither follows.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.deploy_best_practices.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.data_sandbox_refresh.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers requires that all sandboxes that have not been recently refreshed must also receive the newest changes to production. This must be done before any functionality from that environment can be moved to production. Which deployment tool would allow this deployment process to be managed in an automated fashion?
optionA: Change Sets
optionB: Workbench
optionC: Force.com Migration Tool (Ant)
optionD: Force.com IDE
explanation:
The Force.com Migration Tool is the answer because it is the only listed option a machine can run. It is an Ant-based command-line client for the Metadata API, so a build server or scheduler can invoke it with no human present - which is what an unattended, repeatable step that must run before every outbound deployment requires.
None of the others can be driven that way. Change sets are point-and-click by design, Workbench is an interactive browser tool, and the IDE is a developer's workstation environment; each needs somebody clicking through it every time the sync is due.
Currency note: Salesforce retired the Ant Migration Tool in Spring '24. It continues to function but gains no functionality beyond API v59.0, and the Salesforce CLI is the supported command-line client for the same Metadata API today. The reasoning the question tests is unchanged - scriptable API tooling automates, declarative tooling does not - but a pipeline being built now should use the CLI.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/file_based.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/2024/01/moving-on-from-the-ant-migration-tool-to-sf-cli-v2

question: Universal Containers has seven orgs in different regions. Its processes are global and standardized but each region needs the flexibility to be able to understand the global code and customize some aspects for its regions. Which development model is optimized for this need?
optionA: Create a centralized Git with all the code where the global team approves the changes made by the local teams.
optionB: Use unlocked packages to deploy the global code and allow each country to create its own customized unlocked package extensions.
optionC: Use a managed package for global code and another managed package for all regions' code.
optionD: Use a managed package to deploy the global code and allow local teams to request the addition of code within that package.
explanation:
Unlocked packages with extension packages are the package-development pattern Salesforce designed for exactly this scenario: a base unlocked package carrying the global, standardized code/config, plus per-region 'extension' unlocked packages that depend on the base and add region-specific customization. Each region deploys base + its own extension, can read/extend the base, and is in control of its extension's lifecycle.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_unlocked_pkg_intro.htm
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/unlocked-packages-for-customers/break-up-your-metadata

question: Universal Containers is concerned that after each release, reports and dashboards seem to roll back to previous versions. Executives spend many hours crafting these dashboards to perfectly meet their needs, and are now questioning the Salesforce platform's ability to save things, even data records. What can the Salesforce architect advise to stop the rollbacks from happening?
optionA: Ensure report metadata is exported daily and that it is merged into the developer branches before the next release.
optionB: Use a third-party data warehouse.
optionC: Remove the executives' ability to change reports, and only allow developers to do that.
optionD: Back up all the reports just before the release, then reimport them after the release.
explanation:
Nothing is rolling back and no data is being lost - reports and dashboards are metadata, and a deployment overwrites the version in the target org with the version in the payload. The executives edit them in production; the pipeline still carries the older definitions that were captured when the branch was cut; the next release reinstates those. The platform is doing exactly what it was told.
The fix is to make the source reflect reality: retrieve the report and dashboard metadata from production regularly and merge it into the development branches, so the next release carries forward the executives' work rather than replacing it. That is the discipline the org development model is built on - "by externalizing the changes for each release, the team knows that the source repo reflects what they are delivering".
A data warehouse addresses reporting on data, not the loss of report definitions. Taking edit rights away from the executives removes the symptom by removing the capability. And backing the reports up immediately before each release and reimporting afterwards is the same merge done manually, once per release, with no protection against a second team editing in between.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/org-development-model/plan-for-changes-to-your-org2
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/file_based.htm

question: Universal Containers has recently acquired another business that uses Salesforce extensively. UC wants to merge their Salesforce orgs to effectively sell and service customers under one business. Traditionally, UC has followed an Agile development methodology to deliver Salesforce functionality. With the merging businesses, UC is convinced that adopting a Waterfall development methodology is the best approach. Which are two positive aspects of using a Waterfall development methodology? Choose 2 answers
optionA: Changes late in the process are expected and can be handled by integrating them into the requirements specs.
optionB: Milestones, timelines, and estimates tend to be more accurate and predictable due to the upfront due diligence.
optionC: The costs of starting the project are low since much of the design work is pushed to later stages of the process.
optionD: Complex processes that will need to be built are thoroughly understood and documented before coding begins.
explanation:
Waterfall front-loads analysis, and its advantages are the ones that follow from having done that work before anything is built. Complex processes and their interactions are documented and agreed before coding starts, which is valuable exactly when the cost of discovering a dependency late is high. And because scope is settled early, milestones, timelines and estimates rest on something more solid than a guess, which is what makes the plan defensible to a business merging two operations.
The other two statements describe the opposite model. Accommodating change late in the process by folding it into the requirements is Agile's premise - the Agile Manifesto values "responding to change over following a plan" - and Waterfall treats late change as rework against a signed baseline. Nor are Waterfall's start-up costs low: the design effort is the front of the project, not the back.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-agile-basics/learn-the-basics-of-agile
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management

question: When replacing an old legacy system with Salesforce, which two strategies should the plan consider to mitigate the risks associated with migrating data from the legacy system to Salesforce? Choose 2 answers
optionA: Migrate users in phases based on their functions, requiring parallel use of legacy system and Salesforce for a certain period of time.
optionB: Identify the data relevant to the new system, including dependencies, and develop a plan/scripts for verification of data integrity.
optionC: Use a full sandbox environment for all the systems involved, a full deployment plan with test data generation scripts, and full testing including integrations.
optionD: Use a full sandbox environment and perform test runs of data migration scripts/processes with real data from the legacy system.
explanation:
The two keyed answers attack the two ways a migration fails. Scoping the relevant data with its dependencies, and writing the verification scripts in advance, is what turns "the load finished" into "the load is correct" - parent records before children, external ids mapped, record counts and field-level checks proving integrity rather than assuming it. Rehearsing the whole migration in a Full sandbox with the real legacy extract is what exposes everything a design review cannot: the transformations that fail on genuine values, the records that violate validation rules nobody remembered, and the elapsed time of the load against the cutover window. A Full sandbox is the environment for that because it is "a replica of your production org, including all data" and is sized like production.
Phasing users onto the new system in parallel is a cutover strategy - useful, but it manages the business risk of switching over rather than the risk that the data arrives wrong. And rehearsing with generated test data hides precisely the defects a real extract would reveal.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.create_test_instance.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_api_loading_data.htm

question: Universal Containers is delivering many changes to its Salesforce system. Adoption reports are discovering that many features are unused. The steering committee wants this to change and is looking to the architect for advice. What should an architect recommend to overcome this?
optionA: Using Lightning Web Components for every user interface.
optionB: Sending weekly communication emails reporting on least engaged users.
optionC: Adopting user-centered design to understand user needs before building the solution.
optionD: Stop development until current features start being used.
explanation:
Unused features are a discovery failure rather than a delivery failure - the team is building things correctly and building the wrong things. User-centred design moves the discovery upstream: watch how the work is actually done, prototype with the people who will use it, and test usability before committing the build. What ships then matches a need someone has, which is the only durable route to adoption.
The alternatives treat the symptom. A different UI framework changes how a feature is implemented, not whether anyone wanted it. Weekly emails naming the least engaged users apply pressure to individuals for a product problem. Stopping development leaves the same unused features in place and adds a delivery halt to the adoption problem.
Note that this is a design and adoption judgment rather than a platform fact; the references describe the surrounding lifecycle practice and are orienting rather than decisive.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-agile-basics/learn-the-basics-of-agile

question: Universal Containers is in the final stages of building a new application to track custom containers. During a review of the application, a business subject matter expert mentioned that it would be nice to be able to track additional container types beyond what was originally scoped during the plan and design phase. Which two actions should be performed to mitigate the risk? Choose 2 answers
optionA: Have a discussion with the business SME and communicate that a new developer environment will be needed to mitigate the risk.
optionB: Have a discussion with the business SME and communicate that Salesforce has limitations in supporting such a feature to mitigate the risk.
optionC: Escalate and communicate to stakeholders the risk and mitigate it by allocating additional resources to support the new requirement based on stakeholder input.
optionD: Escalate and communicate to stakeholders the risk and mitigate it by extending the timeline of the project to support the new requirement based on stakeholder input.
explanation:
New scope arriving late in the build is a risk to be surfaced, not a decision for the project team to take on the spot. Both keyed actions start the same way - escalate it to the stakeholders with an impact assessment - and then offer the two levers that can absorb it: more resources, or more time. Which one is pulled, or whether something else is dropped instead, is the stakeholders' call because they own the budget and the date.
The two rejected responses both end the conversation at the project team's level. Telling the subject matter expert that a new developer environment is the answer confuses provisioning with scope. Telling them the platform cannot support tracking additional container types is not true - and asserting a platform limitation to avoid a scope conversation is the more damaging of the two, because it closes off a requirement the business may genuinely need.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.deploy_best_practices.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers is planning to release simple configuration changes and enhancements to their Sales Cloud. A technical architect recommends using change sets. Which two advantages would change sets provide in this scenario? Choose 2 answers
optionA: The ability to deploy a very large number of components easily.
optionB: A simple and declarative method for deployment.
optionC: An easy way to deploy related components.
optionD: The ability to track changes to components.
explanation:
For small declarative releases, change sets shine: (B) they are point-and-click — no scripting, no command line — and (C) the 'View/Add Dependencies' button helps roll up related components into one set. They are NOT good at large component counts (A) or change tracking/history (D) — those require source-driven tooling.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.changesets_inbound_deploy.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.changesets_about_connection.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers has development teams working on multiple projects. They are exploring a source control tool to track and manage their code/config. What two benefits does a source control tool provide? Choose 2 answers
optionA: Provides the ability for distributed teams to work in isolation.
optionB: Provides automated code/configuration deployments.
optionC: Provides the ability to automatically identify issues in code/configuration.
optionD: Provides the ability to back up code/configuration changes.
explanation:
Source control's two core benefits: (A) feature branches let distributed teams work independently and merge their changes back together; (D) every commit is a recoverable snapshot, so all code/config history is backed up and reversible. Automated deployment (B) and static analysis (C) are CI/CD and code-quality tools layered on top of source control, not source control itself.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/org-development-model/plan-for-changes-to-your-org2
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) has two major releases every year and the team always runs into longer deployment times. In which two ways can UC reduce deployment time? Choose 2 answers
optionA: Specify the tests to run by using the RunSpecifiedTests test level.
optionB: Use recent deployment validations and the Quick Deploy feature.
optionC: Validate the deployment before migrating components to production.
optionD: Deploy components in groups to reduce deployment time.
explanation:
Two levers actually shorten the deployment window. Choosing RunSpecifiedTests runs only the named tests instead of every test in the org, which is usually where the hours go on a large release. And a deployment that has already been validated against the target org can be promoted with quick deploy, which "takes less time than a standard deploy because it skips running Apex tests. These tests were previously run as part of the validation".
The eligibility window matters when you plan the release: the job ID returned by a validation "is valid for 10 days from when you started the validation". Validate early enough to be inside that window on deployment night and the production step becomes a promotion rather than a fresh test run.
Validating without then using quick deploy simply moves the same work earlier - the real deployment still runs everything again. Splitting the release into groups adds ordering constraints and repeated overhead rather than removing any.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/salesforce-cli-reference/guide/cli_reference_project_deploy_quick.html
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_deploy.htm

question: Which two statements are accurate about why Mock objects are needed when writing test classes? Choose 2 answers
optionA: A Mock is needed whenever the code makes an HTTP callout.
optionB: Mock can also be used on the classes that extend the Batchable interface to bypass the batch jobs.
optionC: Some methods invoke long-running processes; using Mock is a shortcut for bypassing the long executions.
optionD: Using a Mock allows the test class to bypass the dependencies of other objects, methods, state, or behaviors. Therefore, the developer has total control over their own code.
explanation:
The first reason is a platform rule, not a preference: "by default, test methods don't support HTTP callouts, so tests that perform callouts fail", and the documented way through is to "enable HTTP callout testing by instructing Apex to generate mock responses in tests, using Test.setMock". Any code path that makes a callout therefore needs a mock before it can be tested at all.
The second is the general purpose of mocking: it replaces the dependencies a unit under test would otherwise reach - other classes, external services, unpredictable state - with responses the developer chooses, so the test asserts on the logic being tested rather than on whatever the dependency happened to return that day.
The two rejected statements do not describe real mechanisms. Batchable is an interface a class implements, and mocking does not let a test skip the batch execution; the way to exercise batch code in a test is to run it between Test.startTest and Test.stopTest. And shortening a long-running process is a side effect of removing a dependency, not a reason mocks exist.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_restful_http_testing.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexref.meta/apexref/apex_interface_httpcalloutmock.htm

question: Universal Containers is looking to construct a continuous integration process to help manage code quality. Which three tools should be used to enable this? Choose 3 answers
optionA: Force.com Migration Tool (or SFDX CLI)
optionB: Continuous Integration build tool
optionC: Project management tool
optionD: Full sandbox environment
explanation:
CI requires three building blocks: (E) source control to capture every change, (B) a CI build tool (Jenkins, GitHub Actions, Azure DevOps Pipelines, etc.) to run the pipeline, and (A) a deployment tool (Force.com Migration Tool / SFDX CLI) to push metadata into target orgs and run tests. A project management tool (C) supports planning but is not part of CI; full sandboxes (D) are useful but not required to run CI.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/salesforce-cli-reference/guide/cli_reference_project_deploy_start.html

question: Which are two recommended methods of creating test data in Salesforce? Choose 2 answers
optionA: Utilize Heroku Connect to provide test class data.
optionB: Reference data from middleware directly within your test class.
optionC: Host a mock endpoint to produce sample information from an endpoint.
optionD: Load a CSV as a static resource and reference it in a test class.
explanation:
Apex tests are isolated from org data by default, so the records a test needs have to be created by the test. Salesforce documents the static resource route for bulk data: store the records as "a comma-delimited file ending with a .csv extension" whose "first line of the file must contain the field names", then instantiate them in one line with Test.loadData, which "returns a list of sObjects that correspond to each record inserted". That keeps large fixtures out of the Apex and lets QA contribute rows.
For code that calls out, the data has to come from a mock instead, because "test methods don't support HTTP callouts, so tests that perform callouts fail" - an HttpCalloutMock implementation supplies the response the test needs, deterministically.
The rejected options both make a test depend on something outside the org at run time. A test that reads from middleware or a data-sync service is slow, non-deterministic, and fails when the external system does - which in a deployment means the deployment fails.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_testing_load_data.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_classes_restful_http_testing.htm

question: Universal Containers' (UC) Customer Community is scheduled to go live in the EMEA region in 3 months. UC follows a typical centralized governance model. Two weeks ago, the project stakeholders informed the project team about recent changes in mandatory compliance requirements needed to go live. The project team analyzed the requirements and have estimated additional budget needs of 30% of the project cost for incorporating the compliance requirements. Which management team is empowered to approve this additional budget?
optionA: Change Control Board
optionB: Executive Steering Committee
optionC: Project Management Committee
optionD: Security Review Committee
explanation:
The size of the request decides which body answers it. A 30% increase in project cost is a funding decision, and funding sits with the executive steering committee - the sponsors who own the budget and can weigh the extra spend against the consequence of missing a compliance deadline in three months.
The other bodies each own something narrower. A change control board governs what enters the release and whether a change is approved for deployment, working inside the budget that has already been granted. A project management committee runs delivery - plans, resources, and schedules - against that same envelope. A security review committee rules on security posture, which may well be involved in defining what these compliance requirements demand, but is not empowered to fund the work.
Note that this division of authority is organizational governance rather than a documented Salesforce rule; the references orient rather than decide it.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.deploy_best_practices.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) just started configuration and customization of its Salesforce organization. The architect suggested the definition of an Application Lifecycle Management (ALM) process. What are three benefits of following an ALM process? Choose 3 answers
optionA: Training new users after each minor and major release.
optionB: Releasing new features on a consistent schedule.
optionC: Preventing existing working functionality from stopping.
optionD: Avoiding defects from being deployed to production.
optionE: Defining metrics for application development project success.
explanation:
Salesforce frames application lifecycle management as five phases - plan, build, test, deploy, monitor - and says it "provides structure, guiding your changes from initial requirements through deployment and ongoing monitoring". The three keyed benefits are what that structure buys: a predictable release cadence instead of ad hoc pushes, protection for functionality that already works because every change is tested before promotion, and fewer defects reaching production because the pipeline gates them at each stage.
The two rejected options sit outside the process rather than being produced by it. Training users after each release is change management, which a reliable release cadence makes possible but which ALM does not itself perform. Defining what project success means is a governance decision taken before the lifecycle starts.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm

question: Universal Containers has recently replaced a custom service center application with Salesforce Service Cloud. Administrators are now confused about which fields and classes are actively being utilized and how future implementations can be maintained. Choose 2 answers
optionA: Create an adoption plan for end users using Salesforce dashboards and reports.
optionB: Create a governance framework focused on high-level business strategy and goals.
optionC: Create a design standard requiring integration to use declarative configuration patterns.
optionD: Create a governance process requiring all projects to create project deliverable documentation.
optionE: Create a standard method for deprecating classes and fields using design standards.
explanation:
The admins cannot tell what is in use, and both keyed answers create the record that would tell them. Requiring project deliverable documentation as a condition of delivery means each project leaves behind a statement of what it built and why, so the next person inherits intent rather than archaeology. A standard for deprecation handles the other half - the fields and classes that outlived their purpose - by defining how something is marked as going, communicated, and eventually removed, instead of being left in place forever because nobody is certain it is dead.
The rejected options address adjacent problems. An adoption plan measures usage by people, not by metadata. A governance framework aimed at business strategy operates above this question. And requiring integrations to be declarative constrains how things are built without recording what was built or why.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/customfield.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) has two subsidiaries which operate independently. UC has made the decision to operate two separate Salesforce orgs, one for each subsidiary. However, certain functions and processes between the two orgs must be standardized. Which approach should UC take to develop customizations once and make them available in both orgs?
optionA: Develop the functionality in a sandbox and deploy it to both production orgs.
optionB: Create a managed (or unlocked) package in a Developer Edition org and deploy it to both production orgs.
optionC: Create change sets in a sandbox and deploy them to both production orgs.
optionD: Set up Salesforce-to-Salesforce to deploy the functionality from one org to the other.
explanation:
Build the functionality once as a package in a Developer Edition org and install it into both subsidiaries. A package is the mechanism designed for this shape: the standardized functions are versioned centrally, the same version is installed into each org, and later upgrades travel the same path - which is what keeps the two orgs standardized over time rather than only on day one.
Everything else on offer is confined to one org family. A sandbox deploys only to the production org it belongs to, and a change set needs a deployment connection, which exists "between all orgs affiliated with a production org" - so neither can reach two independent production orgs, whatever is built in them. Salesforce-to-Salesforce is a record-sharing feature: it publishes and subscribes to data between orgs and moves no metadata at all.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.changesets_about_connection.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_unlocked_pkg_intro.htm

question: Universal Containers has many development teams deploying into a single org. The business is very seasonal and approaching its busiest season. The business owner asks the architect for advice about its next major production release. What best practice should an architect recommend?
optionA: Make declarative changes in production only.
optionB: Bypass regression testing for minor changes.
optionC: Developers should conduct user acceptance testing.
optionD: Avoid releasing near peak business periods.
explanation:
Salesforce's deployment guidance says this directly: release "at times when most users are off the system", "avoid peak hours when everyone's actively using the system", and steer clear of the period "right before holidays or major events". A seasonal business heading into its busiest weeks is that case exactly - the same defect that would be an inconvenience in a quiet month becomes lost revenue when every user and customer is transacting at once, and the team's capacity to respond is lowest precisely when the stakes are highest.
The rejected options each trade away a control at the moment it is most needed. Making declarative changes directly in production removes the testing that a busy period makes more important, not less. Skipping regression testing for minor changes assumes the minor label is reliable. And having developers run user acceptance testing removes the independent business judgment that acceptance testing exists to provide.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.deploy_best_practices.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000384452&language=en_US&type=1

question: What sandbox type would be appropriate for diagnosing reports of poor performance when accessing certain Visualforce pages?
optionA: Developer Sandbox
optionB: Developer Pro Sandbox
optionC: Full Sandbox
optionD: Partial Copy Sandbox
explanation:
Sandbox Types and Templates names the Full sandbox as the one intended to be used as a testing environment that supports "performance testing, load testing, and staging", because it is "a replica of your production org, including all data, such as object records and attachments, and metadata". Reproducing a slow Visualforce page needs exactly that: view state, query plans and render times all track the data volume behind the page, and Developer (metadata only, 200 MB) and Developer Pro (metadata only, 1 GB) copy no production data at all. A Partial Copy carries only a sample defined by a sandbox template, capped at 10,000 records per selected object, so it cannot reproduce a volume-driven symptom either.
Note also that Salesforce does not permit performance or scale testing in production, so a Full sandbox is not merely the best environment for this work - it is the sanctioned one.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.create_test_instance.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.data_sandbox_environments.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers has a complex deployment coming up. The deployment will include several Apex classes which depend on custom settings that hold important configuration. How should an architect manage this deployment?
optionA: Manually deploy and populate the custom settings in production prior to the Apex class deployment.
optionB: Migrate the configuration to a Custom Metadata Type and include it in the deployment to production.
optionC: Manually deploy and populate custom settings in production using a change set.
optionD: Script the deployment of all functionality via the Force.com Migration Tool.
explanation:
The split that decides this is metadata versus data. Custom metadata type records are metadata: the type and its records both move through change sets, packages and the Metadata API, so the configuration the Apex classes read arrives in the same deployment that delivers the classes. Custom setting records are ordinary data - the definition deploys, the values do not - which is why they have to be recreated in the target org by hand or by a separate load, in a second step that can be forgotten or done wrong.
Moving the configuration to a custom metadata type therefore makes the release self-contained and repeatable across every environment. Populating custom settings manually before the classes land keeps the two-step problem and only reorders it, and scripting the whole deployment changes the tool without changing the fact that the setting values are still data.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.custommetadatatypes_overview.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_custommetadatatypes.htm

question: A Salesforce administrator has initiated a deployment using a change set. The deployment has taken more time than usual. What is the potential reason for this?
optionA: The change set performance is independent of included components.
optionB: The change set includes field type changes for some objects.
optionC: The change set includes new custom objects and custom fields.
optionD: The change set includes changes to permission sets and profiles.
explanation:
A change of field type is not a metadata edit that lands instantly - it triggers a per-record data conversion. Salesforce warns that "the conversion runs in the background" and that "in some cases, the conversion can take over 24 hours to complete", with picklist-to-text and date/time-to-time among the slowest, and deployments also face a ceiling on the total number of field type conversions they can carry. On an org with real data volume that is by far the most likely reason a routine change set suddenly takes hours.
New custom objects and fields are created empty, so there is nothing to convert. Profile and permission set changes rewrite access metadata, which is comparatively cheap. And a change set's duration plainly does depend on what is in it, which is what makes the first option self-refuting.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.notes_on_changing_custom_field_types.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) has multiple teams working on different projects. Multiple projects will be deployed to many production orgs. During code reviews, the architect finds inconsistently named variables and lack of best practices. What should an architect recommend to improve consistency?
optionA: Create a Center of Excellence for release management.
optionB: Use static code analysis to enforce coding standards.
optionC: Require pull requests to be reviewed by two developers before merging.
optionD: Execute regression testing before code can be committed.
explanation:
Inconsistency across many teams is a coverage problem, and only an automated check covers everything. Salesforce ships one for this: Code Analyzer "brings together different code-scanning engines, such as PMD, RetireJS, and ESLint, under a single, unified experience", runs from the CLI so it can be wired "into your build and deployment processes", and supports custom PMD rules for patterns specific to a team's own coding practices. Every commit from every team is then measured against the same rules, whoever wrote it.
The alternatives are weaker at exactly this. Two-reviewer pull requests raise the cost of every change and still vary with whichever two people are reading. A release-management centre of excellence governs process rather than syntax. And regression tests prove behaviour, which is a different property - inconsistently named variables pass every test in the suite.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/salesforce-code-analyzer/guide/code-analyzer.html
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm

question: Universal Containers is building a custom application on the Force.com platform. There is a budget and release date that has been set by the board of directors, but the application must meet the requirements that will be submitted and voted on by a public user community. What is the risk associated with the scenario?
optionA: The project is not using the Waterfall methodology.
optionB: The requirements should not be solicited by an external community.
optionC: The requirements are unknown and the release date has been set.
optionD: The project is not using an Agile methodology.
explanation:
Scope, time and cost cannot all be fixed at once, and here two of the three already are: the board has set the budget and the release date. The third is not merely flexible but unknown - the requirements will be decided later by a public community vote, so nobody can yet say what has been committed to. That is the risk, and it exists before any methodology is chosen.
The two methodology options invert cause and effect. Choosing Agile or Waterfall is a response to this situation, not the risk within it - and neither creates capacity that the fixed date and budget do not contain. Soliciting requirements from an external community is unusual but legitimate; the problem is not where the requirements come from, it is that the commitments were made before they existed.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-agile-basics/learn-the-basics-of-agile
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management

question: Universal Containers (UC) has a customized repository that represents lots of different apps or projects. UC currently is trying to shift from the org development model to the package development model to manage changes. In the org development model, each developer starts their work within their own personal sandbox. When it comes to choosing development environments, what should a Salesforce architect recommend?
optionA: Start using scratch orgs that track all changes automatically and proceed with a staggered approach since scratch orgs can coexist with other models.
optionB: Start using scratch orgs because a developer can spin up a scratch org to start a new project, start a new feature branch, or start automated testing.
optionC: Keep developing in dev sandboxes, so that the developers feel no impact at all as they are used to sandbox development.
optionD: Keep developing in dev sandboxes because scratch orgs are not within the code deployment path.
explanation:
The Salesforce DX Developer Guide defines the scratch org as "a source-driven and disposable deployment of Salesforce code and metadata", and lists the moments to spin one up almost word for word as this option states them: start a new project, start a new feature branch, test a new feature, start automated testing, or start from a fresh org. That is the environment the package development model is built on - the org is described by the project's source and configuration files, so it can be recreated identically by any developer or by a CI job.
Sandboxes remain valid for org-development work, but a sandbox is a copy of an org rather than an expression of source, which is the coupling the package model exists to remove.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_scratch_orgs.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_unlocked_pkg_intro.htm

question: Universal Containers has written several validation rules and workflow rules for the Lead object. Which two test types should an architect suggest to ensure that a large inbound call center does not experience platform slowdowns under high call volume for the Lead object? Choose 2 answers
optionA: Unit Test
optionB: Performance Test
optionC: Load Test
optionD: Stress Test
explanation:
The question is whether the org holds up under call-centre volume, which is what load testing measures - drive the expected concurrent volume at the Lead object and observe whether throughput and response times stay acceptable while every validation and workflow rule fires on each save. Performance testing is the companion measurement, timing the individual transaction so you can tell a slow rule apart from a saturated system.
Unit tests answer a different question entirely: whether the rules are correct, not how they behave under concurrency. Stress testing deliberately pushes past the expected peak to find the breaking point.
Before any of this is scheduled, note the rules Salesforce places on it: "because Salesforce is a multitenant platform, performance testing is not permitted in production environments. Use a full copy sandbox", and tests must be approved in advance - submit the request "at least one week before the testing date", since "unapproved testing is subject to throttling or blocking".
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000387059&language=en_US&type=1
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.create_test_instance.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers is starting a Center of Excellence (CoE). Which two user groups should an architect recommend to join the CoE? Choose 2 answers
optionA: Inside Sales Users
optionB: Call Center Agents
optionC: Executive Sponsors
optionD: Program Team
explanation:
A centre of excellence needs the authority to decide and the capability to carry decisions out, which is what the two keyed groups supply. Executive sponsors bring the mandate, the funding and the ability to settle disputes between business units that no delivery team can settle. The programme team - architects, leads, project managers - is what turns those decisions into standards, reviews and a working pipeline. Salesforce's own org-strategy guidance describes the function in the same terms: a global centre of excellence should manage the business architecture and common standards across all of an enterprise's Salesforce instances.
Frontline groups such as inside sales users and call centre agents are the people the CoE exists to serve, and their input belongs in requirements and design reviews. Seating them on the governing body neither gives them what they need nor gives the CoE what it needs.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/developer-relations/2014/10/enterprise-architecture-multi-org-strategy
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management

question: Universal Containers (UC) has recently acquired other companies that have their own Salesforce orgs. These companies have been merged as new UC business units. The CEO has requested an architect review the org strategy taking into consideration two main factors: (1) The CEO wants business process standardization among all business units. (2) Business process integration is not required as the different business units have different customers and expertise. Which org strategy should the architect recommend in this scenario, and why?
optionA: Single-org strategy, as costs increase as the number of orgs go up.
optionB: Multi-org strategy, as it is uncommon for diversified business units to get used to working in the same space as other business units.
optionC: Single-org strategy, as the high level of business process standardization will be easier to implement in a single org.
optionD: Multi-org strategy, as they could deploy a common managed (or unlocked) package into the orgs of the different business units.
explanation:
Keep the business units in separate orgs and deploy a common managed or unlocked package into each one. That package is what carries the standardized processes: they are built once centrally and installed into every unit's org, so the processes stay identical without merging orgs that share no customers.
Salesforce's org-strategy guidance reaches this directly. The decision rests on the enterprise operating model, whose two axes are business process standardization and business process integration, and the CEO's two statements place this company in the Replication quadrant - standardization high, integration explicitly not required. For that quadrant the guidance is that companies "can (and probably should) have multiple orgs, however you should consider deploying a managed package from a central org into all of the replicated business units".
Consolidating into one org is the recommendation for the Unification and Coordination quadrants, where process integration is high. It is not high here: the business units have different customers and different expertise, so a merge buys the complexity of one org serving many lines of business and none of the shared-data benefit that would repay it.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/developer-relations/2014/10/enterprise-architecture-multi-org-strategy

corrected.note: Answer moved C to D. Salesforce's operating-model guidance maps high standardization with no integration requirement to the Replication quadrant, whose documented recommendation is multiple orgs plus a managed package deployed from a central org - not a single org.

question: Universal Containers (UC) is embarked on a large Salesforce transformation journey. UC's DevOps team raised a question about tracking Salesforce metadata throughout the development lifecycle across sandboxes all the way to production. As the deployment architect of the project, what should be the recommendation to track which version of each feature is in different environments?
optionA: Use an AppExchange or third-party tool that is specialized in Salesforce deployment.
optionB: Use change sets to track deployed customizations.
optionC: Use an Excel sheet to track deployment steps and document the SFDX commands.
optionD: Use Salesforce SFDX commands to deploy to different sandboxes.
explanation:
The question is not how to move metadata but how to know where each feature currently sits. Change sets and the CLI both deploy without recording a pipeline-level history, and a spreadsheet is accurate only until the next deployment nobody logs. What the DevOps team is describing - an environment map, per-feature version state, deployment history and diffs between orgs - is the function of a purpose-built release management product layered over the same APIs.
Currency note: Salesforce now ships DevOps Center as a native option, and it appears alongside change sets and the Metadata API in Salesforce's own list of ways to deploy changes. It provides source-tracked work items and a pipeline view without a third-party licence, so an org choosing tooling today should evaluate it before the AppExchange products this item points to.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.deploy_overview.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers' (UC) development team is using an Agile tool to track the status of build items, but only in terms of stages. UC is not able to track any effort estimates, log any hours worked, or keep track of remaining effort. For what reasons should UC consider using the Agile tool for effort tracking?
optionA: Allows the management team to manage the performance of bad developers who are slacking off.
optionB: Allows the developer to compare their effort estimates and actuals to better adjust their future estimates.
optionC: Allows the organization to track the developer's work hours for salary compensation purposes.
optionD: Allows the management team to make critical timeline commitments based solely on developer estimates.
explanation:
Effort tracking earns its place by improving the team's own forecasting. Recording an estimate, then the actual, then the remaining effort gives the developer the feedback loop that makes the next estimate better, and gives the team a velocity stable enough to plan with. That is the inspect-and-adapt habit applied to estimation rather than to the product.
The three rejected reasons all repurpose estimates as a management instrument, and each one destroys the data that makes the practice work. Using estimates to identify developers who are slacking teaches the team to pad every estimate. Tracking hours for compensation turns a planning tool into a timesheet. And committing to a timeline based solely on developer estimates treats a forecast with known variance as a promise, which is how a team ends up defending an estimate rather than reporting reality.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/scrum-and-kanban-at-salesforce/learn-about-scrum
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-agile-basics/learn-the-basics-of-agile

question: The CTO at Universal Containers is complaining to the software development managers that he has no visibility of their teams' work status. What two software development methodologies should an architect suggest to solve this issue, and why? Choose 2 answers
optionA: DevOps, because monitoring and logging practices help you stay informed of performance in real time.
optionB: Kanban, because one of its basic elements is to make everything visible, creating consistent transparency of work items.
optionC: Scrum, because openness is one of the five core Scrum values.
optionD: Waterfall, because it defines a fixed schedule and duration for each activity.
explanation:
The complaint is about visibility of work status, and two of these frameworks are built on exactly that. Salesforce's own description of Kanban states it directly: "one of the basic elements of Kanban is to make everything visible, creating consistent transparency of work items" - work is written onto cards, the workflow is mapped into columns, and the position of every card shows its state at a glance, so "it's easy for teams to know when delays occur". Scrum reaches the same place through its ceremonies and values: teams are expected to be transparent about progress and to speak up when assumptions turn out wrong, and the inspect-and-adapt cadence puts that in front of everyone on a fixed rhythm.
Waterfall publishes a schedule, which is a plan rather than a status - it says what should be happening this week, not what is. And DevOps monitoring reports on how the deployed system is performing, which is a different subject from where the teams' work has got to.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/scrum-and-kanban-at-salesforce/learn-about-kanban
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/scrum-and-kanban-at-salesforce/learn-about-scrum

question: Universal Containers (UC) is planning for a huge data migration as part of their Service Cloud implementation. UC has approximately 15 million customers, 30 million contacts, and 30 million active cases. Which two key areas of UC's data migration test plan should be included? Choose 2 answers
optionA: Target Salesforce server and source system IP addresses.
optionB: Manual and automated data validation approaches.
optionC: Success criteria for data migration.
optionD: APIs to be used for data migration.
explanation:
A test plan needs (C) explicit success criteria — what 'good' looks like (record counts match, key fields populated, integrity checks pass, throughput within window) — and (B) the validation methods (automated count/checksum/field-level checks plus manual spot-checks) that will be used to test against those criteria. IP addresses (A) and API choices (D) are infrastructure/design, not test-plan content.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp.meta/salesforce_large_data_volumes_bp/ldv_deployments_best_practices_api_loading_data.htm
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.create_test_instance.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers wants to introduce data volume testing to resolve ongoing performance defects earlier in the lifecycle. Regulations prohibit the use of production data in non-production environments. Which two options can the architect recommend? Choose 2 answers
optionA: Use Query Analyzer in production.
optionB: Request a partial sandbox copy after the next Salesforce release.
optionC: Generate mock data that mimics production data shape and volume.
optionD: Perform data masking on a Full sandbox after a refresh.
explanation:
Both keyed options reach production-like volume without moving regulated data downstream. Salesforce Data Mask runs "in full or partial sandboxes" and is installed as a managed package in production, with the masking job executing only in the sandbox so production is never touched; the result cannot be unmasked, which is what makes a masked Full sandbox safe to hand to a testing team. Generating synthetic data that mirrors production's row counts and distribution reaches the same volumes with no real records involved at all.
A Partial Copy refresh still copies real production records, so it does not satisfy the regulation, and Query Analyzer in production inspects query plans rather than providing an environment to test in.
Currency note: the article is now titled "Secure Your Sandbox Data with Salesforce Data Mask (Legacy)". The managed package reaches end of service on 31 December 2026 and Salesforce directs customers to Data Mask & Seed. The masking approach is unchanged; the product name is not.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.data_mask_overview.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.create_test_instance.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) is considering updating their Salesforce production deployment as a part of their release management process. Which three best practices should UC consider for production deployment? Choose 3 answers
optionA: Define a rollback strategy.
optionB: Announce the maintenance window ahead of time.
optionC: Alert all users on the day of deployment.
optionD: Temporarily suspend configuration changes in production.
explanation:
The three keyed practices cover the three things that go wrong on deployment night. A rollback strategy has to be designed in advance, because reversing a release is not a single command - restoring changed components means redeploying the previous state, and removing new ones means a destructiveChanges manifest naming them. Announcing the maintenance window ahead of time lets users plan around it, which is also the point of Salesforce's advice to release when most users are off the system. And freezing configuration changes in production during the window keeps an administrator's edit from colliding with the release - the platform enforces part of this itself, since a deployment takes an org lock that blocks setup changes until it completes.
Alerting users on the day of the deployment is the same communication too late to be acted on. Aligning releases with Salesforce's own upgrades stacks two sources of change on one weekend, which makes any resulting defect harder to attribute, not easier.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.deploy_best_practices.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_deploy_deleting_files.htm
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000384452&language=en_US&type=1

question: Universal Containers (UC) is a high-tech company using SFDX tools and methodologies for its Salesforce development. UC has moved some of its code and configuration to unlocked packages. Which two best practices should an architect recommend to support UC's new package development strategy? Choose 2 answers
optionA: Test developed packages in test environments before installing to production.
optionB: Move everything in the existing codebase to a single monolithic package.
optionC: Consult the Metadata Coverage report to identify features supported by packages.
optionD: Version control does not need to be used, as packages manage all the code and configuration.
explanation:
Two habits keep a package strategy honest. Install each package version into a scratch org or sandbox before it reaches production - installation exercises dependencies, namespace resolution and version ordering, none of which the build step proves. And check the Metadata Coverage Report, which lists every metadata type against the channels that can carry it, including Metadata API, change sets, unlocked packaging, managed packaging and source tracking; it is how you find out that a component you intended to package cannot be packaged before the split is designed around it.
The rejected options invert the model. One monolithic package restores the single tangled unit that packaging exists to break up, and version control is more important under package development, not less - the package version is built from source, so the repository is the record of what a version contains.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/metadata-coverage
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_unlocked_pkg_intro.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) has been following the Waterfall methodology to deliver customer apps in Salesforce. As the business is growing at scale and with demand to incorporate features and functionality at faster pace, UC is finding the Waterfall approach is not optimal, and intends to transition towards an Agile development methodology. Which are two strengths of using an Agile development methodology? Choose 2 answers
optionA: Careful documentation is done at each step of the process so a target body of knowledge is available for inspection.
optionB: The project requirements in later phases are expected and accommodated by the process, by design.
optionC: All elements of the build are fully understood before work begins, reducing risk of unpleasant surprises.
optionD: There are many small releases of functional code, allowing stakeholders to see and touch the work in progress.
explanation:
Agile's two strengths here are the ones the Agile Manifesto states as values. Requirements that arrive later are handled by design rather than treated as a breach of the plan - "responding to change over following a plan" - which is what a business growing at scale needs when next quarter's requirement is not yet known. And the work is delivered in many small increments, so stakeholders see and use working functionality early instead of waiting for a single delivery at the end: "working software over comprehensive documentation".
The two rejected statements describe what the Manifesto was reacting against. Careful documentation at every step and a full understanding of the whole build before work begins are the strengths of the "document-heavy, design-it-all-up-front process" the Agile signatories identified as the source of large, expensive, often-aborted projects.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-agile-basics/learn-the-basics-of-agile

question: Ursa Major Solar (UMS) has used Aura components significantly in its Salesforce application development. UMS has established a robust test framework and the development team follows Salesforce-recommended testing practices. The UMS team uses Salesforce's test tool to check for common accessibility issues. In which two environments can the UMS team call Aura accessibility tests? Choose 2 answers
optionA: WebDriver Test
optionB: JS Test (Jasmine)
optionC: AuraDriver Test
optionD: ACCTEST
explanation:
Salesforce answers this in one sentence: "You can call Aura accessibility tests in two environments. For JavaScript tests, use $A.test.assertAccessible(). For WebDriver tests, use auraTestingUtil.assertAccessible()." Both evaluate the rendered DOM against Salesforce's accessibility rules and return an empty string on success or the failing rules on failure, so the same checks run whether the component is exercised from a JavaScript test or driven through a browser.
The two rejected options are not environments the framework provides - there is no AuraDriver test type and no ACCTEST harness. Naming the method that belongs to each environment is what the question is really testing, since calling the JavaScript form from a WebDriver test does not work.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.lightning.meta/lightning/accessibility_write_tests.htm

question: Cloud Kicks (CK) is launching a new sneaker line during the upcoming holiday season and needs to do thorough batch data testing before go-live. CK is using Salesforce Unlimited Edition. What two sandbox types should the architect recommend for batch data testing? Choose 2 answers
optionA: Developer Sandbox
optionB: Partial Copy Sandbox
optionC: Developer Pro Sandbox
optionD: Full Sandbox
explanation:
Batch testing requires real data volumes. Only Partial Copy (B) and Full Copy (D) sandboxes carry production data — Partial via a sandbox template with up to 5 GB; Full as a complete replica. Developer (A, 200 MB) and Developer Pro (C, 1 GB) hold no production data and can't realistically test batch jobs.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.create_test_instance.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.data_sandbox_environments.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) has four different business units (BUs) with different processes that share global customers. They have implemented a multi-org strategy with one org consolidating customer 360-degree view, and four orgs for the different BUs. Each of the BU orgs reads and writes customer information from/to the customer 360-degree view org in real time. UC is now launching a new BU that will use Salesforce. It does not share customers with the other BUs and needs flexibility in their business processes. What should an architect recommend as org strategy for this new BU?
optionA: Use the same Salesforce org of another BU that shares geographical localization with the new BU.
optionB: Use a new Salesforce org for the new BU, and customize integration so that it reads and writes customer information from the customer data org.
optionC: Use a new stand-alone Salesforce org for the new BU, not integrated with the others.
optionD: Deploy the new BU in the customer 360-degree view org, and read/write customer information from it without need of custom integration.
explanation:
On the operating-model framework Salesforce uses for org strategy, this new business unit is low on both axes: it shares no customers with the others, so there is no process integration to preserve, and it needs its own processes, so there is no standardization to enforce. That is the Diversification quadrant, where the guidance is that such companies "will probably always have multiple orgs" because the work to consolidate different business processes and data models into one org "is usually very complicated".
A stand-alone org therefore gives the new unit full autonomy at no cost to anyone else.
