Wiring it into the customer 360 hub, or deploying it inside that hub, buys integration for records that do not overlap; reusing another unit's org imposes that unit's processes on a business chosen for its flexibility.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/developer-relations/2014/10/enterprise-architecture-multi-org-strategy

question: Universal Containers (UC) works with different partners and has few admin resources that take care of the day-to-day deployment tasks. As a result, UC would like to find a way to automate the deployments using Metadata API. Which two limitations of Metadata API should be considered when using Metadata API-based deployments? Choose 2 answers
optionA: Deploy and retrieve up to 10,000 files at once.
optionB: Maximum size of deployed .zip file is 400 MB.
optionC: Maximum size of deployed .zip file is 39 MB.
optionD: Deploy up to 10,000 files, but retrieve more than 10,000 files.
explanation:
Salesforce documents both keyed limits in the same place: "You can deploy or retrieve up to 10,000 files at once", and "the maximum size of the deployed or retrieved .zip file is 39 MB". Base-64 encoding inflates the payload, so the compressed archive has to stay under roughly that figure before encoding to fit inside the SOAP message limit.
That also settles the two distractors. The file cap applies symmetrically to deploy and retrieve, so no option that lets retrieve exceed it is correct, and 400 MB is not the archive limit under any reading.
One figure to have right: the companion limit on the uncompressed contents is "600 MB or 629,145,600 bytes", not 400 MB. Both constraints apply at once - a package can fail the uncompressed ceiling while its .zip is comfortably under 39 MB.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.salesforce_app_limits_cheatsheet.meta/salesforce_app_limits_cheatsheet/salesforce_app_limits_platform_metadata.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_deploy.htm

corrected.note: Answer stands. The old explanation taught the uncompressed limit as 400 MB; Salesforce documents it as 600 MB (629,145,600 bytes). The 39 MB .zip figure it gave is correct.

question: What are two limitations an architect should consider when designing a strategy for managing technical reference data with multiple related objects? Choose 2 answers
optionA: Apex CPU limits
optionB: Circular relationships
optionC: HTTP response size
optionD: Depth of nested relationships
explanation:
Both keyed limits are design-time constraints on the shape of the reference data itself. Relationship queries cannot traverse indefinitely: "in each specified relationship, no more than five levels can be specified in a child-to-parent relationship", and there are ceilings on breadth too - no more than 55 child-to-parent relationships and no more than 20 parent-to-child relationships in a single query. A reference model nested more deeply than that cannot be read in one query no matter how the code is written. Circular relationship chains are the other structural trap: a cycle among related reference objects cannot be loaded or traversed in a defined order.
One version detail worth carrying: the parent-to-child depth moved. It is up to five levels in API version 58.0 and later, but only two levels in 57.0 and earlier, so a query that works today can fail against an older manifest version.
Apex CPU time and HTTP response size are real limits, but they bind at run time on a particular transaction rather than constraining how the reference data may be modelled.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.soql_sosl.meta/soql_sosl/sforce_api_calls_soql_relationships_query_limits.htm

question: Northern Trail Outfitters (NTO) recently acquired Eastern Trail Outfitters (ETO). NTO's sales leadership team had hands-on experience with ETO's Sales Optimization app and have given the feedback that the app would benefit NTO's sales team. Which option should the architect recommend for having ETO's Sales Optimization app in NTO's Salesforce org in the shortest possible time?
optionA: Create an unmanaged package of the app and deploy in NTO's org.
optionB: Create users in ETO's org and provide access to NTO's sales team.
optionC: Create a core team and build the Sales Optimization app in NTO's org.
optionD: Create a managed package of the app and deploy in NTO's org.
explanation:
The question sets one criterion - shortest possible time - and an unmanaged package is the mechanism Salesforce documents for exactly this situation: unmanaged packages are used "for distributing open-source projects to developers, or as a one-time drop of applications that require customization after installation". Build the package from the app already running in ETO's org, install it in NTO's org, and the components land as ordinary metadata that NTO's admins can then edit.
A managed package is built for a different job: it is the format "used by Salesforce partners to distribute and sell applications to customers", and it requires a globally unique namespace registered for the packaging org before anything can be uploaded. That is setup work this transfer does not need, and it buys the wrong outcome - installed managed components are locked against modification in the subscriber org, so NTO's own team could not adapt the app they just acquired. Creating users in ETO's org leaves the sales team working in the wrong system, and rebuilding the app is the slowest path of all.
The trade the unmanaged route accepts is that the publisher "can't change or upgrade" an unmanaged package after installation - there is no upgrade channel back to ETO. For a one-time transfer of an app NTO is taking ownership of, that is the intended behaviour rather than a loss.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.packagingGuide.meta/packagingGuide/packaging_developing_unmanaged.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.pkg1_dev.meta/pkg1_dev/sharing_apps.htm

corrected.note: Answer moved D to A. Salesforce documents the unmanaged package as the one-time drop of an application that is customized after installation, which is this scenario and the fastest route. A managed package targets partner distribution, needs a registered namespace first, and locks its components against edits in the installing org - so it is both slower to produce and wrong for an app NTO will now own and modify.

question: Universal Containers has just acquired Planetary Storage. Both companies use Salesforce to manage their sales activities. The two companies have many customers in common and the company plans to merge the two sales organizations, but the products and sales processes between the two original companies will remain different and distinct. What factor should the company consider in merging the two Salesforce orgs into a single org?
optionA: Transactional sales data could be combined without modification since standard objects are used.
optionB: Business processes on standard objects can be merged without modifications.
optionC: Customer data could be merged with modifications using standardization and de-duplication.
optionD: Salespersons selling both product lines would need two logins, one for each product line.
explanation:
Many shared customers means shared customer records exist in both orgs with conflicting/duplicate data. The merge requires standardization (canonical formats for names, phones, addresses, IDs) and de-duplication (matching rules + duplicate rules + manual review). Sales data (A) and processes (B) cannot just be combined — they're different in each company. Two logins (D) defeats the purpose of merging.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/developer-relations/2014/10/enterprise-architecture-multi-org-strategy
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?language=en_US&id=sales.managing_duplicates_overview.htm&type=5

question: Universal Containers has just initiated a project to implement a custom container tracking application with a large development team. The project manager is concerned that the large number of developers in a single Developer Pro sandbox could lead to challenges with code being overwritten. Which two methods should be used to mitigate this risk? Choose 2 answers
optionA: Replace the Developer Pro sandbox with a Partial Copy sandbox.
optionB: Provide each developer their own sandbox/developer org and implement a code repository and continuous integration to merge code into the Developer Pro sandbox.
optionC: Provide each developer their own sandbox/developer org and implement managed packages to deploy to the merge.
optionD: Use a single sandbox and strictly coordinate development across shared components, and implement a code repository to allow developers to merge code into a common repository.
explanation:
The risk is two developers editing the same component in one org, where the second save silently wins - there is no merge step in a sandbox. The primary answer removes the shared surface: give each developer their own environment, so their work is isolated until they commit, and let the repository and continuous integration perform the merge into the shared Developer Pro sandbox. That is the standard org development arrangement, where each team member customizes in their own Developer sandbox and the source repo becomes the record of what is being delivered.
The fallback answer accepts a single environment but still adds the repository, which is what gives the team a history to recover from and a place to resolve conflicts, plus explicit coordination over the components more than one person touches.
Swapping the sandbox type changes the data it holds and nothing about concurrent editing. Managed packages are a distribution format, not a mechanism for merging one team's in-progress work with another's.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/org-development-model/plan-for-changes-to-your-org2
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.create_test_instance.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) has a huge volume of metadata that cannot be deployed at once. What is the recommended strategy for UC to be successful with the deployment?
optionA: Use a continuous integration tool such as Jenkins to deploy in the right order.
optionB: Identify metadata dependencies, create logical groupings, and deploy in the right order.
optionC: Use a combination of the Ant Migration Tool and change sets for deployment.
optionD: Sort and group the metadata alphabetically and deploy them in the same order.
explanation:
Large deployments fail because of dependency cycles and ordering — not because of the tool used. Map the dependency graph, partition metadata into deployable bundles (e.g., custom objects/fields → Apex → page layouts → reports), and deploy in dependency-respecting order. The choice of tool (A, C) is secondary; alphabetical ordering (D) ignores dependencies.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.deploy_best_practices.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/file_based.htm

question: Universal Containers is about to begin the release of a major project. To facilitate this, they have several sandboxes to make their deployment train. These sandboxes are a mix of preview and non-preview instances. What should the architect recommend?
optionA: No advice needed, mixing instance types is important for regression testing.
optionB: Refresh all non-preview sandboxes during the release preview window.
optionC: Contact support to roll back the release when Salesforce upgrades the sandboxes.
optionD: Refresh all non-preview sandboxes when the release management team has time.
explanation:
A preview sandbox sits on an instance that takes the next Salesforce release early; a non-preview sandbox stays on the release production is running. Carrying a deployment train across both means components are built and tested against two different platform versions at once.
The documented lever is the refresh itself. During the transition between major releases Salesforce creates preview sandboxes by default - to get a non-preview sandbox in that window you must have the option enabled by Salesforce support and then explicitly choose Request Non-Preview. So refreshing the non-preview sandboxes inside the preview window is what brings the whole train onto the same release.
Rolling a sandbox back off the new release is not something support does, and refreshing whenever the release management team has time is how the split arose in the first place.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.data_sandbox_preview.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers operates from North America and does business within North America. UC has just acquired a local company in Asia to start operating from Asia. Currently, these two business units operate in two different languages. Both units have different sales processes and have to comply strictly with local laws. During the expansion phase, UC would like to focus on innovation over standardization. What should an architect recommend given the scenario?
optionA: Single-org strategy, standardized sales process, common rules, and business-unit-specific locale.
optionB: Multi-org strategy, standardized sales process, common rules, and same locale across orgs.
optionC: Single-org strategy, standardized sales process, common rules, and same locale for all business units.
optionD: Multi-org strategy, each org has its own sales process, common rules, and operates in its own locale.
explanation:
Every fact in the scenario pushes the same way on Salesforce's operating-model framework for org strategy: different sales processes and a stated preference for innovation over standardization put the business low on standardization, and two units serving separate territories under different local law share no process integration. That is the Diversification quadrant, where the guidance is that these companies "will probably always have multiple orgs" - the work to force different business processes and data models into one org "is usually very complicated".
The three rejected options all standardize the sales process, which is the one thing the business explicitly said it does not want during the expansion phase, and one of them additionally imposes a single locale on units that operate in different languages.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/developer-relations/2014/10/enterprise-architecture-multi-org-strategy

question: Universal Containers is validating an outbound change set from the Developer sandbox to the production org. Which two locking behaviors will occur during a deployment? Choose 2 answers
optionA: The sandbox org will be locked. Administrators cannot modify metadata.
optionB: The production org will be locked. Users will still be able to read/write data to the org.
optionC: The production org will be locked. Administrators cannot modify metadata during this time.
optionD: The production org will be locked. Users can only read data during this time.
explanation:
A deployment takes an org lock on the target, and the lock is over metadata rather than the org as a whole. Salesforce describes the behaviour directly: administrative changes that affect large numbers of records - including metadata deployments - lock the relevant setup area so that simultaneous conflicting changes cannot corrupt data or metadata, and the lock is self-resolving with no manual removal. So an administrator attempting a setup change against production while the deployment runs meets an Org Administration Locked error.
Nothing in that stops ordinary work. Users keep reading and writing records throughout, which is why a production deployment does not require an outage window for the business.
The source org is not involved. A change set is validated and deployed against the target, so the sandbox it came from stays fully editable.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000384452&language=en_US&type=1
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.changesets_inbound_deploy.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) is embarking on a large program of work, with different projects and different vendors. UC created a Center of Excellence (CoE) that is struggling with scope creep between the different projects. What role should the architect suggest be added to the CoE?
optionA: Change Manager
optionB: Release Manager
optionC: Product Owner
optionD: Scrum Master
explanation:
Scope creep BETWEEN multiple projects and vendors is a cross-project change-control problem, which is the Change Manager's remit within a CoE. The Change Manager owns the change-control process — reviewing, approving, and gatekeeping change requests across the whole program — so they can hold the line on scope across projects rather than within one. Product Owner (C) governs backlog and priorities within a single product/project and has no authority across projects, so it doesn't address creep between them. Release Manager (B) handles the deployment pipeline; Scrum Master (D) facilitates a single team and has no authority over scope. Note: the certification exam treats Change Manager here as change-control governance, not user-adoption change management.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/developer-relations/2014/10/enterprise-architecture-multi-org-strategy
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management

question: Which two decisions should be made by an Architecture Review Board (ARB)? Choose 2 answers
optionA: What testing tools should be used to track integration testing requirements.
optionB: Whether to utilize the Waterfall or Agile methodology on the project.
optionC: Whether to implement Single Sign-On with SAML or delegated authentication.
optionD: Whether to create a new Salesforce object or override an existing object using a new record type.
explanation:
An architecture review board rules on decisions that are expensive to reverse and that constrain everything built afterwards. Choosing between SAML single sign-on and delegated authentication is one: it fixes how identity is established for every user and integration, and unwinding it later touches every connected system. So is deciding whether a requirement becomes a new custom object or a record type on an existing one - that choice propagates into sharing, reporting, automation and every integration that queries the object, and it is very costly to change once data exists.
The other two decisions belong elsewhere. Which testing tool tracks integration requirements is a delivery-tooling choice. Whether the project runs Agile or Waterfall is a methodology decision for the sponsor or steering committee - it shapes how the work is organized, not how the system is built.
Note that the division of authority between an ARB and other governance bodies is organizational practice rather than a documented Salesforce rule; the references orient rather than decide it.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.deploy_best_practices.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers wants to implement a release strategy with major releases every four weeks and minor releases every week. Major releases follow Development, System Testing (SIT), User Acceptance Testing (UAT), and Training. Minor releases follow Development and User Acceptance Testing (UAT) stages. What represents a valid environment strategy consideration for UAT?
optionA: Minor and major releases use separate Developer Pro sandboxes.
optionB: Minor and major releases use the same Full Copy sandbox.
optionC: Minor releases use a Partial Copy sandbox and major releases use a Full Copy sandbox.
optionD: Minor releases use a Developer sandbox and major releases use a Full Copy sandbox.
explanation:
The decisive constraint is the refresh interval, not the size of the release. A Full sandbox can be refreshed only every 29 days, which cannot serve a UAT environment feeding weekly minor releases; a Partial Copy refreshes every 5 days and carries a sample of production data defined by a sandbox template, which is enough to accept a small change. Major releases every four weeks fit the Full sandbox cadence, and they are the ones that need a production-sized, fully populated org to be accepted in.
That also rules out sharing one Full Copy across both cadences: a single Full sandbox cannot be refreshed on a weekly rhythm at all. Developer Pro and Developer sandboxes copy metadata only, so no business user can run acceptance testing against real data in them.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.data_sandbox_environments.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/2014/12/salesforce1-enterprise-environment-management

question: Universal Containers (UC) has a large backlog of work. They have noticed that despite their best efforts, valuable enhancements and updates are not being completed because they do not have the bandwidth to get them done. Many of these items are low effort and would not require experienced resources. What should the architect recommend that will minimize additional costs and allow UC to accomplish more?
optionA: UC should start a citizen development program.
optionB: UC should eliminate low-value items from the backlog.
optionC: UC should hire additional resources to reduce the backlog.
optionD: UC should hire a partner to complete the needed backlog items.
explanation:
The constraint is stated in the question: the outstanding items are low effort, do not need experienced resources, and the answer must not add cost. Hiring staff or engaging a partner both fail the last test directly. Dropping the items fails the first - they are described as valuable enhancements, so removing them from the backlog resolves the queue by discarding the value.
A citizen development programme is the option that adds capacity without adding spend: business users build the low-risk, declarative items themselves inside guard-rails that IT sets - naming and design standards, a review step, a defined boundary for what a citizen developer may touch and what must come to the platform team. The governance is what separates it from ungoverned admin sprawl, and it is the part that has to be designed rather than assumed.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.deploy_best_practices.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A technical lead is performing all code reviews for a team and is finding many errors and improvement points. This is delaying the team's deliveries. Which two actions can effectively contribute to the quality and agility of the team? Choose 2 answers
optionA: Create development standards and train teams in those standards.
optionB: Choose the most senior developer to help the technical lead in the code review.
optionC: Skip the code review and focus on functional tests and UAT.
optionD: Use a static code analysis tool in the pipeline before manual code review.
explanation:
The bottleneck is one person catching problems that should never have reached them, so both answers move work off that person. Written standards plus training change what developers submit - the recurring findings become habits rather than review comments. A static analyser in the pipeline catches the mechanical half automatically: Salesforce's own Code Analyzer unifies engines such as PMD, RetireJS and ESLint, runs from the CLI so it fits "into your build and deployment processes", and supports custom rules for a team's own conventions. What reaches the technical lead is then design and logic, which is the part that actually needs their judgment.
Adding a second senior reviewer doubles the reviewing capacity without reducing the volume of findings, and it removes another experienced developer from delivery. Skipping review entirely trades a delivery delay for defects found later, at higher cost, by users.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/salesforce-code-analyzer/guide/code-analyzer.html
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) is looking for advice on how often it should refresh its sandboxes. UC currently uses a development lifecycle that starts with developer environments and moves to integration testing, QA testing, UAT, and then production. They have many scrum teams working concurrently and the teams do not agree on when refreshes should occur. What two recommendations should the architect suggest? Choose 2 answers
optionA: Integration sandboxes should be refreshed rarely because of the burden of maintaining the various API connections.
optionB: Sandboxes should be refreshed on the day when the refresh is allowed for that type of sandbox.
optionC: Development environments should generally be refreshed after each working feature has been successfully migrated.
optionD: Production is the only pristine environment.
explanation:
Both keyed options come straight from Salesforce's environment-management guidance. Of the developer sandboxes it says: "I typically expect these sandboxes to be refreshed after a working feature has been successfully migrated upstream" - so a developer starts each new piece of work from the state that was just proven upstream. And it states the governing principle for every other environment: production is your only pristine environment, which is why refreshes only ever flow from production outward and every downstream org is understood to be drifting.
The same source rejects the integration-sandbox option rather than supporting it: it recommends refreshing the system integration sandbox "as often as is practical", and for that reason advises against using a Full sandbox there, since its 29-day refresh limit is too slow. Refreshing on whatever day the interval first allows lets the calendar rather than the delivery pipeline decide.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/2014/12/salesforce1-enterprise-environment-management
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.data_sandbox_environments.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: Answer stands. The old explanation conceded that the integration-sandbox option "is sometimes argued" and that frequent integration refreshes break partner connections. The source it rests on says the opposite: refresh the system integration sandbox as often as is practical, and avoid a Full sandbox there precisely because 29 days is too infrequent.

question: Cloud Kicks is considering using an automated testing tool to help manage deployments between environments. When should the architect recommend the use of an automated testing tool?
optionA: Automated tests should be run daily in all developer orgs.
optionB: Automated tests should be run only when merging into Full or Partial Copy sandboxes.
optionC: Automated tests should be run daily in all developer orgs, and when branches are merged.
optionD: Automated tests should be run when branches are merged.
explanation:
Best practice is to run automated tests both as a scheduled daily build (catches environment drift, scheduled-job interactions, regressions) AND on every merge to the integration branch (gates broken code from reaching shared environments). Restricting tests to merges into higher sandboxes only (B) lets bugs accumulate at lower tiers.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/salesforce-code-analyzer/guide/code-analyzer.html

question: Universal Containers (UC) is developing a new Customer Community. Requirements for the Community are not fully defined. UC is planning on using an Agile methodology for this work and has promised delivery of the complete system in three months. What are two risks associated with this approach? Choose 2 answers
optionA: Agile does not allow for changes to requirements, so customers might not like the resulting solution.
optionB: Agile is not an appropriate development methodology for Customer Community implementations.
optionC: Given the lack of requirements and the three-month timeline commitment, the project may not be feasible.
optionD: The functionality that can be delivered in 3 months is unknown, and may not meet the needs of the business.
explanation:
Agile flexes scope against a fixed time and cost, and this commitment has removed the flex while leaving the scope undefined. Both risks follow from that. Nobody can say today whether a complete system is achievable in three months, because there is no agreed definition of complete - so the feasibility of the promise is unknown rather than optimistic. And whatever does fit inside the window will be decided by prioritization as the work proceeds, which means the delivered functionality may not be the functionality the business needed.
The two rejected statements are wrong about Agile itself. Changing requirements is what the method is designed to accommodate - the Agile Manifesto values "responding to change over following a plan" - and nothing about a customer community makes it unsuitable for iterative delivery.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-agile-basics/learn-the-basics-of-agile
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management

question: Universal Containers has decided on a single-org strategy, despite having to deal with the complexity of having multiple lines of business (LOBs) inside a single org. What are two common challenges in a single-org strategy for multiple LOBs? Choose 2 answers
optionA: Lack of declarative sharing and visibility capabilities to ensure correct visibility of objects and records.
optionB: Making Salesforce work with multiple currencies.
optionC: Apex design will need to be mature and adhere to strict guidelines to support a large enterprise model.
optionD: The data model becomes more complex as the scope in the org increases.
explanation:
Both keyed options are the challenges Salesforce's own org-strategy guidance names for a single org serving many lines of business: "Your data model becomes much more complex and controversial as you increase your scope in the org", and "Your apex design will need to be very mature to support a large enterprise model" - every line of business shares one execution context, so trigger frameworks, governor limits and separation of concerns have to be engineered rather than left to convention.
The two distractors describe capabilities the platform handles well: sharing and visibility are configured declaratively through the role hierarchy, sharing rules and territories, and multi-currency is a standard org setting with dated exchange rates.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/developer-relations/2014/10/enterprise-architecture-multi-org-strategy

question: Universal Containers (UC) operates globally from different geographical locations. UC is revisiting their current org strategy. Which three factors should an architect consider for a single-org strategy? Choose 3 answers
optionA: Consistent processes across the business.
optionB: Increased ability to collaborate.
optionC: Fewer interdependencies.
optionD: Centralized data location.
explanation:
Single-org strategy is favored when: (A) the business runs consistent processes everywhere (one config fits all), (B) collaboration across regions is high (one org, one chatter, one search), and (D) centralized data is desired (a single 360 view of every customer). 'Fewer interdependencies' (C) and 'tailored implementation' (E) actually argue for multi-org.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/developer-relations/2014/10/enterprise-architecture-multi-org-strategy

question: Universal Containers (UC) has a large user base (>300 users) and was originally implemented eight years ago by a Salesforce systems integration partner. Since then, UC has made a number of changes to their Visualforce pages and Apex classes in response to customer requirements, made by a variety of vendors and internal teams. Which three issues would a new technical architect expect to see when evaluating the code in the Salesforce org? Choose 3 answers
optionA: Custom-built JSON and string manipulation classes that are no longer required.
optionB: Multiple unit test failures would be encountered.
optionC: Broken functionality due to Salesforce upgrades.
optionD: Multiple triggers on the same object, making it hard to understand the order of operations.
optionE: Duplicated logic across Visualforce pages and Apex classes performing similar tasks.
explanation:
Eight years of changes by rotating vendors produces accretion, and the three keyed findings are its structural signatures. Hand-rolled JSON and string-parsing utilities are redundant because Apex has native support - System.JSON serializes and deserializes Apex objects directly, with createParser and createGenerator for lower-level work - so code predating that survives as dead weight. Multiple triggers on one object is the classic consequence of successive teams each adding their own rather than extending what exists, and the platform gives no guarantee about the order in which they fire. And logic duplicated across Visualforce pages and Apex classes is what happens when each vendor builds beside the previous work instead of refactoring it.
A caution about the two options this item excludes: they are not impossible, only not the findings you would predict from this history. Unit test failures are common in long-lived orgs, usually because tests depend on org data or hardcoded ids rather than because a release broke them. And Salesforce's versioning commitment applies to code pinned to an API version - it is not a promise that an upgrade can never affect existing behaviour, which is precisely why release preview windows and regression testing in an upgraded sandbox exist.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexref.meta/apexref/apex_class_System_Json.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_triggers_order_of_execution.htm
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.data_sandbox_preview.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: Answer stands. The old explanation ruled out two options by claiming Salesforce's backward-compatibility guarantee means platform upgrades never break existing unit tests. That is not what versioning promises, and it contradicts two other questions in this deck, which key on refreshing into the release preview window and regression testing an upgraded sandbox precisely because a release can break existing behaviour.

question: Which are two characteristics of an effective communication plan? Choose 2 answers
optionA: Consistent communication to a pre-defined list of stakeholders.
optionB: Communication to stakeholders on a 'need-to-know' basis.
optionC: Requesting feedback for outstanding architectural questions.
optionD: Reporting project status, timelines, and impacts.
explanation:
A communication plan is judged on predictability and content. Predictability means a named list of stakeholders who each know what they will receive and when, so nobody has to ask and nobody is surprised. Content means the substance stakeholders need to make decisions - status against plan, timelines, and the impacts of what has changed since the last update, including the bad news.
The two rejected characteristics fail on those tests. Communicating on a need-to-know basis makes each disclosure a judgment call by the sender, which produces exactly the surprises that erode trust. And soliciting feedback on open architectural questions is real work that should be happening, but it is a design activity carried out with specific people, not a property of the plan that keeps the project's stakeholders informed.
Note that this is communication practice rather than a platform fact; the reference is orienting rather than decisive.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management

question: Universal Containers has just initiated a project involving a large distributed development and testing team. The development team members need access to a tool to manage requirements, and the testing team needs access to a tool to manage defects. Additionally, stakeholders are requesting ad-hoc status reports. What tool should an architect recommend to support the project?
optionA: Wave (Tableau CRM)
optionB: Code Repository
optionC: Spreadsheets
optionD: Project Management Tool
explanation:
Three needs are described - requirements for the developers, defects for the testers, and ad hoc status for stakeholders - and they are three views of the same underlying work items. A project management tool holds all of them in one place, which matters most for a distributed team: the requirement, the defect raised against it, and the status report drawn from both stay connected without anyone reconciling separate systems.
The alternatives each cover one slice at best. A code repository versions the source and can link a commit to a work item, but it does not manage requirements or defect workflow. An analytics platform reports on data it is given and does not capture the work. Spreadsheets can hold a list, but they have no workflow, no concurrent editing discipline for a distributed team, and no live status for stakeholders to pull.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm

question: Universal Containers is in the process of testing their integration between Salesforce and their on-premise ERP systems. The testing team has requested a sandbox with up to 10,000 records in each object to benchmark the integration performance. What is the fastest approach an architect should recommend?
optionA: Spin off a Developer sandbox, migrate the metadata, and load the data using Data Loader.
optionB: Spin off a Full Copy sandbox with all the objects that are required for testing the integration.
optionC: Spin off a Developer Pro sandbox, migrate the metadata, and load the data using Data Loader.
optionD: Spin off a Partial Copy sandbox using a sandbox template with all the objects required for testing the integration.
explanation:
The requirement names the Partial Copy sandbox's documented limit almost exactly: a Partial Copy carries "standard and custom object records and Attachments up to 5 GB, with a maximum of 10,000 records per selected object", with the objects chosen through a sandbox template. So the testing team's 10,000 records per object arrive automatically on creation, with no data load to build or run.
A Full sandbox would also hold the data but copies the entire production database and takes far longer to provision and refresh, and the question asks for the fastest approach. Developer and Developer Pro sandboxes copy metadata only, so both of those options end in a manual Data Loader run for every object.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000381868&language=en_US&type=1
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=sf.data_sandbox_templates.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.create_test_instance.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) is considering updating their Salesforce release management process. Which three best practices should UC consider for version control? Choose 3 answers
optionA: Maintain a single entry point for production from the master branch.
optionB: Maintain unrestricted access to the release sandboxes for all changes being deployed.
optionC: Maintain separate developer branches for minor and major releases.
optionD: Automation is a must with various application branches in the repository.
optionE: Maintain a single repository for the application with individual branches for projects.
explanation:
Three version-control best practices: (A) one trunk/main branch is the single source of truth for production deploys; (C) separate branches isolate minor (fast-track) and major (longer-running) work so they don't entangle; (E) one repo per application with a branch per project keeps related artifacts together. Unrestricted sandbox access (B) is the opposite of governance, and 'automation is a must' (D) is true but not specifically a version-control practice.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/org-development-model/plan-for-changes-to-your-org2
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) uses a managed package to install an internal Sales app in five orgs. Within each org there are integrations and local processes with the objects of the managed package. UC wants to use unlocked packages for better integration with CI/CD processes. What would the Salesforce architect recommend for this migration?
optionA: Export all data from objects/fields of the managed package, uninstall it, install an unlocked package with the same namespace as the managed package, and restore all data.
optionB: Export all data from objects/fields of the managed package, uninstall it, install the unlocked package without a namespace, and restore all data.
optionC: Do not change to unlocked packages, as it is possible to perform all CI/CD processes with the managed package.
optionD: Migrate all classes, Visualforce, and components from the managed package to the unlocked package. Install the new version of the managed package (objects/fields only) and the unlocked package with the other components.
explanation:
The two options that begin by uninstalling are disqualified by what uninstalling costs. Salesforce's own conversion procedure spells out the sequence - export all the data from the package's objects, uninstall it, install the replacement, and import the data back - and across five orgs carrying live integrations and local processes built on those objects, that is a destructive migration, not a tooling change. Doing nothing is not an answer either, since the goal is to bring the code under CI/CD.
That leaves splitting the package by layer: leave the data model where it is, so the objects, fields and every integration and local customization bound to them keep their identity, and move the classes, pages and components into an unlocked package that can be built from source on every commit.
Plan the removal carefully, because taking components out of a released managed package is a controlled operation rather than a simple edit - Salesforce supports removing metadata components from second-generation managed packages through a documented process, and in most cases removal marks the component deprecated rather than hard-deleting it from subscriber orgs.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.pkg1_dev.meta/pkg1_dev/convert_to_managed_package.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.pkg2_dev.meta/pkg2_dev/sfdx_dev_dev2gp_remove_md_components.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_unlocked_pkg_intro.htm

question: Northern Trail Outfitters (NTO) has well-defined release management processes for both large and small projects. NTO's development team created a workflow and a trigger for changes in its opportunity renewal process. What should the architect recommend for release planning of these changes?
optionA: Plan this as an interim release after checking with Salesforce Support.
optionB: Plan this as a major release and align with a Salesforce major release.
optionC: Plan this as a minor release with training and change management.
optionD: Plan this as a patch release and align with a Salesforce patch release.
explanation:
Size the release to the change. A workflow rule and a trigger on the opportunity renewal process is a small, well-bounded piece of work, so it belongs in the minor release stream rather than being held for a major one. What it is not is invisible: it changes what sales users see when they renew an opportunity, so it needs training and change communication to go with it. That pairing - minor release, real change management - is what the answer captures.
Aligning it with a Salesforce major release would be worse on both counts. It delays a small change for months, and it lands the org's change at the same moment as the platform's, so any resulting defect is harder to attribute. Salesforce upgrades arrive on Salesforce's schedule and are not a release slot a customer can book, and neither an interim category cleared with Support nor a patch aligned to a Salesforce patch describes a real planning option here.
Currency note: Workflow Rules reached end of support at the end of 2025, with Flow as the replacement, so equivalent automation built today would be a record-triggered flow.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.deploy_best_practices.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.data_sandbox_preview.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: What is the responsibility of the technical architect within a Change Control Board meeting?
optionA: Approve the upcoming release for deployment into production.
optionB: Prioritize the Salesforce product roadmap with business stakeholders.
optionC: Troubleshoot deployment errors that occurred during the last release.
optionD: Conduct code reviews for projects in the development phase.
explanation:
A change control board exists to decide whether a change may proceed, and each seat brings one kind of authority to that decision. The technical architect's is technical: whether the release is sound enough to go to production - its design, its risk, its dependencies, its rollback path - and the meeting is where that judgment is recorded as an approval or a rejection.
The three rejected activities are all real architect work happening somewhere else. Prioritizing the product roadmap with business stakeholders is a planning forum. Troubleshooting errors from the last release is incident work that may produce input to this meeting but is not conducted in it. And code review belongs in the development flow, well before a release reaches a control board - if code quality is first examined at the CCB, the gate is in the wrong place.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.deploy_best_practices.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management

question: Universal Containers wants to do weekly releases to production. What approach will mitigate the risk of bugs being inadvertently introduced to production?
optionA: Use of an Agile methodology.
optionB: Automated testing.
optionC: User acceptance testing.
optionD: Requirements traceability.
explanation:
Weekly releases require a regression suite that runs in minutes, not days — manual UAT (C) and tracing (D) won't scale to that cadence. Automated testing (unit + integration + UI smoke) gates each release in a CI pipeline, blocking regressions before they reach production. Methodology (A) sets cadence but doesn't catch bugs.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_code_coverage_intro.htm

question: Which two project situations favor a Waterfall methodology? Choose 2 answers
optionA: An application in post-production, with incremental changes made by a small team.
optionB: An application with many systems and inter-dependencies between components.
optionC: An application with regulatory compliance requirements to be validated by outside agencies.
optionD: An in-house application with a fixed team size, but an open timeline and flexible requirements.
explanation:
Waterfall pays for itself when the cost of getting the design wrong is higher than the cost of designing it all first. Many systems with dependencies between components is one such case - interfaces, data flows and sequencing have to be agreed across teams before anyone builds, because a late change in one component ripples through the others. Regulatory requirements validated by an outside agency is the other: the phase artefacts and traceable documentation Waterfall produces are the evidence the validation runs on, and an iterative process that leaves that documentation until later has nothing to submit.
The two rejected situations are where iterating is cheap and change is expected. A live application taking incremental changes from a small team can ship, learn and adjust continuously, and an in-house project with an open timeline and flexible requirements has no fixed baseline for Waterfall to protect.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-agile-basics/learn-the-basics-of-agile
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management

question: Universal Containers (UC) has received feedback from the field on several new feature requests aligned to business goals. UC is looking for a way to quickly get feedback and prioritize these requests. Which two options should an architect recommend? Choose 2 answers
optionA: Create the backlog or priority list in a project management tool.
optionB: Present the feature requests at a Center of Excellence meeting.
optionC: Send the requests to IT for a formal review at the end of the year.
optionD: Bring the feature request to the Test Manager to gain quality checks.
optionE: Create design standards around the new features being requested.
explanation:
Prioritization needs a list and a forum, and the two keyed options supply one each. A single backlog in a project management tool is what lets requests be compared against each other rather than each being argued on its own merits as it arrives. The centre of excellence is where that ranking is decided against business goals by people with the standing to decide it - Salesforce's org-strategy guidance describes the CoE as the body that manages business architecture and common standards across the enterprise, which is the authority this needs.
The rejected options fail the speed requirement or the purpose. A formal IT review at year end is the opposite of quick feedback. Quality checks and design standards both matter, but they govern how a request is built once it has been accepted, not whether it should be.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/developer-relations/2014/10/enterprise-architecture-multi-org-strategy
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management

question: Universal Containers has a highly integrated environment with significant process orchestration between systems. When refreshing UAT, objects that have External IDs from production no longer point to valid External IDs in the UAT environment. What should an architect do to resolve this?
optionA: Let UAT point to production integrations and roll back each transaction after it finishes.
optionB: Delete all the data and use an automated testing tool to create new data across all the systems in UAT.
optionC: Mask the External ID so nobody can see the production value.
optionD: In the post-refresh plan, modify External IDs to a known valid set of values for UAT.
explanation:
A refresh copies production values wholesale, so every External ID in the refreshed org still names a record in the connected production systems. Left alone, UAT orchestration reaches straight back into production-equivalent records - which is why rewriting those identifiers belongs in the post-refresh plan alongside endpoints, credentials and named credentials.
Salesforce provides the hook for it: an Apex class implementing the SandboxPostCopy interface runs "at the end of the sandbox copy using a special Automated Process user", and the documented uses are exactly this kind of preparation - create users, "run sanitizing code on records", and perform other setup tasks. Scripting the External ID remap there makes it repeatable on every refresh rather than a manual step someone forgets.
Pointing UAT at production integrations and rolling transactions back is the risk itself, deleting all data throws away the production-like shape the refresh was for, and masking the value only hides it from users - the integration still sends it.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexref.meta/apexref/apex_interface_System_SandboxPostCopy.htm
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.data_sandbox_refresh.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: What are two advantages of automated test data loads over manual data loads? Choose 2 answers
optionA: Automated loads can be done with no human oversight.
optionB: Automated loads are reliable in their results.
optionC: Automated loads will increase costs.
optionD: Automated loads cannot be scripted by CI/CD tools.
explanation:
(A) Once scripted, automated loads run unattended (overnight, on schedule, in CI), no operator required. (B) They produce identical, repeatable results every run — a key property for testing. (C) is a disadvantage, not an advantage; (D) is false — CI/CD tools script Data Loader / Bulk API operations routinely.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_testing_load_data.htm

question: The team at Universal Containers is building an application on Java that will interact with its Salesforce application. They want to use SOQL queries to retrieve and make changes to smaller pieces of Salesforce metadata through this application. Which API should the team leverage?
optionA: Tooling API
optionB: User Interface API
optionC: Metadata API
optionD: Any Salesforce API
explanation:
The requirement names the Tooling API's defining feature. Salesforce describes it as giving "fine-grained access to an org's metadata", where "Tooling API's SOQL capabilities for many metadata types allow you to retrieve smaller pieces of metadata" and "smaller retrieves improve performance, which makes Tooling API a better fit for developing interactive applications" - which is precisely a Java application querying and amending individual metadata components.
The Metadata API works the other way: deploy() and retrieve() "move metadata (XML files) between a Salesforce org and a local file system" in bulk, with no SOQL against metadata at all. The User Interface API returns records and the layout information needed to render them, not metadata definitions.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_tooling.meta/api_tooling/intro_api_tooling.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/file_based.htm

question: What is the responsibility of an executive sponsor on a project?
optionA: Communicate project status.
optionB: Determine project methodology.
optionC: Approve changes to project scope.
optionD: Design executive dashboards.
explanation:
The executive sponsor owns the project's business case and its funding, and scope is what connects those two things - a change to scope changes the cost, the date, or the benefit being claimed. So approving scope changes is the responsibility that follows directly from what the sponsor holds.
The rejected duties belong to people the sponsor relies on. Communicating status is the project manager's job, and the sponsor is one of its recipients. Methodology is a delivery decision, made against criteria the governance bodies set. And building executive dashboards is implementation work that a sponsor may commission but does not perform.
Note that role definitions of this kind are organizational practice rather than a documented Salesforce rule; the reference is orienting rather than decisive.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management

question: Universal Containers is about to begin development work on a new project in their Salesforce org that will take many months to complete. UC is concerned about how critical bugs will be addressed for existing live functionality. What is the recommended release management strategy to address this concern?
optionA: Include fixes for critical bugs in the ongoing development sandboxes so that they will be released with the other code.
optionB: Utilize a dedicated Developer Pro sandbox to address critical bugs and release to production.
optionC: Address critical bugs in the development sandboxes and push those changes to production separately.
optionD: Keep teams separate until the end of the project and create a Full Copy sandbox to merge their work then.
explanation:
A long-running project and a production defect move on different clocks, so they need different paths to production. Salesforce's environment-management guidance names a dedicated environment for exactly this - a production fix sandbox generated for urgent defects only, holding the minimum needed to reproduce and correct the problem. The fix is built and tested there, deploys to production on its own, and is then merged back into the project work so the long-running branch picks it up.
Every alternative couples the two. Fixing critical bugs inside the ongoing development sandboxes means the fix cannot ship until the project does, which is months away. Fixing them there and then pushing those changes to production separately sounds targeted but drags whatever else that sandbox contains toward production with it, since the environment holds months of unfinished work. And keeping the teams apart until the end and merging in a Full Copy sandbox postpones every integration problem to the worst possible moment.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/2014/12/salesforce1-enterprise-environment-management
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.create_test_instance.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Which statement is true for a Staging sandbox in a typical release pipeline?
optionA: Salesforce major releases (e.g., Winter to Spring) always occur in Staging and Production at the same time.
optionB: The Staging environment can only be updated once every two weeks.
optionC: The Staging sandbox is automatically refreshed on a schedule set by the administrator.
optionD: When created or refreshed, the Staging sandbox is a full replica of Production.
explanation:
Salesforce names staging as a Full sandbox use case directly: the Full sandbox is "intended to be used as a testing environment" supporting "performance testing, load testing, and staging", and it is "a replica of your production org, including all data, such as object records and attachments, and metadata". So at the moment it is created or refreshed, a staging sandbox mirrors production - which is the whole point of the final pre-production rehearsal.
The other statements fail on documented behaviour. A sandbox can sit on a preview instance and take the next major release weeks ahead of production, so staging and production are not always on the same version. There is no administrator-scheduled auto-refresh; a refresh is requested manually. And the interval that governs a Full sandbox is 29 days, not two weeks.
References:

question: Universal Containers (UC) is implementing a governance framework and has asked the architect to make recommendations regarding release planning. Which two decisions should the architect make when planning for releases? Choose 2 answers
optionA: Whether Salesforce will wait to upgrade the pod until after a UC release is complete.
optionB: When to test a new UC feature release if there are issues.
optionC: How to test existing functionality to ensure no regressions are introduced.
optionD: How to roll back to the previous Salesforce release if there are issues.
explanation:
Release planning decides what the team will do, so both keyed decisions are about the team's own process: when a feature release gets retested if defects are found, and how existing functionality is regression tested so the release does not break what already works. Those are choices with real trade-offs - the size of the regression suite, what is automated, how much re-test a late fix triggers - and nobody else can make them.
The two rejected options ask for control the customer does not have. Salesforce upgrades its instances on its own schedule, and the customer-facing lever is the preview window - a preview sandbox "provides early access to new features and lets you test your configurations before the production upgrade" - which is a way to get ahead of the upgrade rather than to postpone it. For the same reason there is no route to roll a Salesforce release back. Plan around the upgrade calendar; do not plan to move it.
