question: A year has passed since a project has gone live and a developer is looking to make an update to an existing Apex class, but is unsure of its purpose. What artifact from the original project should be leveraged to determine the purpose of the class?
optionA: User Acceptance Test Scripts.
optionB: Test Execution Plan.
optionC: Requirements Traceability Matrix.
optionD: Test Sign Off Document.
explanation:
The developer needs to know why the class exists, which is a requirements question rather than a testing one. A requirements traceability matrix is the artefact that carries that link: each requirement is mapped forward to the design elements and components that implement it and to the tests that verify it, so a class can be traced back to the business need that produced it a year ago.
The three rejected artefacts all describe testing rather than intent. Acceptance test scripts say what a tester did, an execution plan says how and when tests were run, and a sign-off document records that someone accepted the result. Any of them may mention the feature by name, but none states why the code was written.
Worth pairing with the practice that would have avoided the problem: the field and object description attributes are metadata and travel with the component, so intent recorded there stays attached to the thing it describes.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/customfield.htm
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management

question: Why does Salesforce prohibit Stress Testing against Production?
optionA: There is not enough CPU.
optionB: It is a shared environment.
optionC: It is blocked by data center infrastructure.
optionD: It causes Internet congestion.
explanation:
The reason is architectural rather than technical: production is shared infrastructure, so a test designed to drive one org to its breaking point degrades service for every other tenant on the same instance. Salesforce states the rule directly - "because Salesforce is a multitenant platform, performance testing is not permitted in production environments. Use a full copy sandbox", and "scale tests are only permitted in sandboxes".
The prohibition comes with a process rather than a flat refusal. Testing in a sandbox needs prior approval, submitted "at least one week before the testing date" with a test plan, dates, the sandbox org id and the scenario, and "unapproved testing is subject to throttling or blocking".
The rejected options invent physical causes - a shortage of CPU, a network block, congestion - where the actual constraint is the obligation Salesforce has to its other customers on that instance.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000387059&language=en_US&type=1
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.create_test_instance.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) has a recruiting application using Metadata API version 35, deployed to production last year. The current Salesforce platform is running API version 36. A new field introduced on the object Apex page in API version 36 has been developed by a UC developer, who tries to deploy the page using the previous deployment script that uses API version 35. What will happen during the deployment?
optionA: The deployment script will pass because the new field is backward compatible with the previous API version 35.
optionB: The deployment script will fail because the new field is not known for the previous API version 35.
optionC: The deployment script will pass because the new field is supported on the current platform version.
optionD: The deployment script will fail because the platform does not support the previous API version 35.
explanation:
A deployment is validated against the API version declared in its manifest, not against whatever the platform happens to be running. A field introduced in the later version does not exist in the earlier version's schema, so a script pinned to the older version cannot describe it and the deployment fails on an unknown field. Raising the version in package.xml is the fix, and it is the only fix - the platform's own version does not rescue a manifest that claims an older one.
The option blaming platform support is a different claim, and a checkable one: Salesforce supports each API version "for a minimum of 3 years from the date of first release", and the currently retired band is versions 21.0 through 30.0, retired as of Summer '25 (7.0 through 20.0 went in Summer '22). Versions 31.0 and above remain supported, so an older-but-supported version is a real scenario rather than an impossible one - which is exactly why the manifest version is where the failure comes from.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_rest.meta/api_rest/api_rest_eol.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_deploy.htm

question: The CTO at Universal Containers decided to implement the Scrum framework for its agile teams and communicated a set of Scrum principles to the company. Which describes a Scrum principle?
optionA: Deliver working software, so if a software component is working, avoid changing it.
optionB: Respect other teams by not doing their work (a developer should not test the software).
optionC: Create transparency by being honest and clear about timing, planning, and obstacles.
optionD: Embrace change by working on a different scope every day.
explanation:
Transparency is the principle being described, and it is foundational to Scrum rather than incidental: teams are expected to be honest and clear about timing, progress, plans and obstacles, to speak up when help is needed, and to report back when an assumption turns out to be wrong. That visibility is what makes inspection possible, and inspection is what makes adaptation possible - each sprint's inspect-and-adapt point depends on the previous one having been reported truthfully.
The three rejected statements each invert something. Avoiding change to working software contradicts continuous improvement. Refusing to test because testing is someone else's work contradicts the cross-functional team, where the team as a whole is accountable for a done increment. And changing scope daily is not embracing change - the sprint exists precisely so that change is absorbed between sprints rather than during them.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/scrum-and-kanban-at-salesforce/learn-about-scrum
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-agile-basics/learn-the-basics-of-agile

question: Universal Containers (UC) has multiple teams with major projects working concurrently in their own developer sandboxes. After deploying to production, a bug is discovered. Due to tight timelines, the development team has suggested correcting the bug in the user acceptance testing (UAT) environment, which is a full copy sandbox. What should the architect recommend? Choose 2 answers
optionA: UC should spin up a new sandbox to use as a hotfix environment and deploy the fix from there to production.
optionB: The fix should be made in the developer environment where the project work was done.
optionC: Since the issue was found in production, it should be treated as a change request and go through the change control process.
optionD: Correcting the bug in UAT is ideal since UAT is a full copy and will be the fastest.
explanation:
Two things are wrong with fixing the bug in the user acceptance testing sandbox, and the keyed answers address one each. First, the environment: UAT is in use, and building an emergency fix there disturbs the testing other people are relying on while mixing the fix into whatever else that environment holds. A sandbox stood up as a hotfix environment isolates the change so that what reaches production is the fix and nothing else - Salesforce's environment-management guidance describes exactly this, a sandbox generated for urgent defects only.
Second, the governance: a defect discovered in production is a production change like any other. Tight timelines change how quickly the change control process runs, not whether it runs - the approval, the record of what was deployed and the rollback plan are what make the fix reversible if it makes things worse.
Speed is a real constraint here, but the option that treats UAT as the fastest route is measuring only the first step and ignoring the contaminated test environment and the unapproved production change it leaves behind.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/2014/12/salesforce1-enterprise-environment-management
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.deploy_best_practices.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: There are many types of quality assurance techniques that can help minimize defects in software projects. Which two techniques should an architect recommend for Universal Containers to incorporate into its overall CI/CD pipeline? Choose 2 answers
optionA: Business verification testing.
optionB: Stress testing.
optionC: Automated browser testing.
optionD: Static code quality analysis.
explanation:
A CI/CD pipeline can only include techniques that run unattended on every change, and both keyed answers qualify. Static analysis runs at commit time against the source: Salesforce's own Code Analyzer unifies engines such as PMD, RetireJS and ESLint behind one CLI command, is designed to be integrated "into your build and deployment processes", and reports violations before the code has executed. Automated browser tests run after the deployment step and exercise the assembled application through the UI, which is the only layer that catches a break between components that each pass their own unit tests.
The two rejected techniques both need something the pipeline cannot supply. Business verification testing needs business users making judgments, which happens after a release reaches them. And stress testing is not permitted against production at all, and needs advance approval even in a sandbox, so it cannot sit in a pipeline that runs on every merge.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/salesforce-code-analyzer/guide/code-analyzer.html
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000387059&language=en_US&type=1
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm

question: Salesforce has three major releases a year. Which type of change introduced by a release can cause automated browser tests to need updating?
optionA: DOM changes.
optionB: New standard fields.
optionC: Metadata schema changes.
optionD: New Apex methods.
explanation:
Automated browser tests (Selenium, WebDriver-based) navigate and assert on the rendered HTML Document Object Model (DOM). When a Salesforce release changes the HTML structure, CSS class names, or element IDs — collectively DOM changes — the selectors in automated tests break and require updating. New standard fields (B), metadata schema changes (C), and new Apex methods (D) do not affect the DOM structure that browser tests use.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.lightning.meta/lightning/lightning_testing_intro.htm
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.data_sandbox_preview.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) is using Sales and Service Cloud. They have two major releases and four minor releases every year, and maintain deployment (dev), integration, user acceptance (UAT), staging, and hotfix sandboxes. What should an Architect recommend when UC has P1 issues that must be fixed immediately?
optionA: Fix the issue in staging and deploy it into production.
optionB: Fix the issue in the hotfix sandbox, test, and deploy to production.
optionC: Fix the issue in development, test in UAT, and deploy to production.
optionD: Follow the release management process to move to production.
explanation:
The organization has already built the answer: a hotfix sandbox is one of the environments it maintains, and it exists precisely so that a production emergency has a path that does not run through the release pipeline. Salesforce's environment-management guidance describes the same environment - a sandbox for urgent defects only - and the discipline that goes with it: fix, test, deploy, then merge the fix back into the in-flight release work so the next release does not undo it.
The rejected routes each borrow an environment that is doing something else. Staging is holding the validated state of the next planned release, so deploying a fix from there ships that release early. Development to UAT to production is the full pipeline, which is correct for planned work and too slow for a P1. And following the standard release process is the right answer to a different question - the point of a defined hotfix path is that emergencies are handled by an agreed exception rather than by suspending governance.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/2014/12/salesforce1-enterprise-environment-management
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.create_test_instance.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers has an active production org and is planning to release new features next month. The team is preparing a deployment plan and reached out to the technical architect for inputs on the rollback strategy. What should a technical architect recommend?
optionA: Backup the existing metadata using the ANT Migration Tool. To roll back, deploy again to production using backed-up metadata.
optionB: Create a sandbox from production to take backup of existing metadata. To roll back, manually delete new components and redeploy using metadata from this sandbox.
optionC: Create a sandbox from production to take backup of existing metadata. To roll back, use destructiveChanges.xml to delete new components and redeploy original metadata from the sandbox.
optionD: Backup the existing metadata using the ANT Migration Tool. To roll back, manually delete new components and deploy again using backed-up metadata.
explanation:
A rollback has two halves, and only one of them is a redeploy. Restoring the changed components is straightforward - deploy the pre-release metadata captured beforehand. Removing components the release added is not, because a deployment never deletes anything: the Metadata API only removes what a destructiveChanges.xml manifest names, alongside a package.xml that lists no components and carries the API version. Scripting that removal is what makes the rollback repeatable and reviewable, where deleting components by hand in Setup is unrepeatable and easy to get wrong under pressure.
Taking the backup as a sandbox created from production gives a complete, self-consistent snapshot of the pre-deployment state to redeploy from, rather than a retrieval whose completeness depends on the manifest someone wrote at the time.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.api_meta.meta/api_meta/meta_deploy_deleting_files.htm
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.create_test_instance.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) is implementing Service Cloud for their contact centers for 3,000 users and approximately 10 million customers. The average expected response time is less than 5 seconds with 1,500 concurrent users. What type of testing will help UC measure the page response time?
optionA: Unit testing.
optionB: Load testing.
optionC: System integration testing.
optionD: Stress testing.
explanation:
The requirement is a response time at a stated concurrency - under 5 seconds with 1,500 concurrent users - which is the definition of a load test: drive the expected volume and measure what the system does at that volume. Unit tests establish correctness at any scale, integration testing establishes that the systems exchange data correctly, and neither produces a page response time.
Stress testing is the near miss. It deliberately exceeds the expected peak to find where the system fails, which answers a different question, and it cannot be run where the users are: "performance testing is not permitted in production environments. Use a full copy sandbox", with tests approved in advance and unapproved testing "subject to throttling or blocking". Plan the load test in a Full sandbox, sized like production, and submit the request before booking the window.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000387059&language=en_US&type=1
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.create_test_instance.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: What three tools should an architect recommend to support application lifecycle management methodology? Choose 3 answers
optionA: Database management systems.
optionB: Version control repository.
optionC: Middleware.
optionD: Continuous integration tool.
explanation:
The three keyed tools are the ones the lifecycle cannot run without. A version control repository holds the source and its history, and it is what makes the source rather than an org the record of what is being delivered. A continuous integration tool is what executes the build, the tests and the deployment on every change instead of when someone remembers. An issue tracking tool holds the work itself - the stories and defects that the plan and build phases operate on - which is what connects a deployed change back to the request that caused it.
The two rejected options are infrastructure rather than lifecycle tooling. A database management system sits under an application, and middleware moves data between systems at run time; neither participates in planning, building, testing or releasing a change.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/org-development-model/plan-for-changes-to-your-org2

question: Universal Containers (UC) is preparing for the new Salesforce release in a couple of months and has several ongoing development projects that may be affected. Which three steps should the team at UC take to prepare for this release? Choose 3 answers
optionA: Contact Salesforce to schedule a time to upgrade the full sandbox.
optionB: Refresh a sandbox during the Release Preview Window to ensure they have the upcoming release.
optionC: Run regression tests in an upgraded sandbox to detect any issues with the upgrade.
optionD: Review the release notes for automatically-enabled features and technical debt.
optionE: Upgrade any SOAP integrations to the newest WSDL as early as possible.
explanation:
The three keyed steps are the release-readiness loop. Refreshing a sandbox inside the release preview window puts it on an instance that takes the next release early - during that window Salesforce creates preview sandboxes by default - which gives the team a version of the platform production will not see for weeks. Regression testing there is what converts that access into information, and reading the release notes catches the features that switch themselves on and the behaviour changes no test was written for.
The two rejected steps misplace who controls what. Upgrade timing is set by Salesforce and cannot be scheduled by the customer. And a SOAP integration keeps working against the WSDL it was built on, since older API versions remain supported; regenerating it is work you do when you want something new, not release preparation.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.data_sandbox_preview.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers is building a new complex integration to a legacy system. The legacy system is also going through a major upgrade. Senior leadership has committed to the board that the combined programs will be completed on time. What is the risk with this plan?
optionA: The deadline is scheduled during a Salesforce release.
optionB: The project team has decided to use the Waterfall methodology.
optionC: The legacy system team is using an Agile methodology.
optionD: Multiple work-streams with dependencies could impact the go-live.
explanation:
The risk is the dependency between two work-streams running at once. The integration is being built against a legacy system that is itself being upgraded, so the interface it targets is moving while it is being built - a slip or a design change on either side lands on the other, and the commitment made to the board covers both programmes as one date. That coupling is what makes the plan fragile, and managing it needs an explicit joint plan: agreed interface contracts, aligned milestones, and a shared view of what happens to the combined date if either side moves.
A Salesforce release falling near the deadline is a scheduled, published event that can be planned around, and the preview window exists so a team can test against the new version in advance. The methodology each team has chosen is a way of organizing work, not a risk in itself - two teams can deliver on different methods provided the dependencies between them are managed.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/salesforce-application-lifecycle-management-quick-look/learn-about-salesforce-application-lifecycle-management
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.data_sandbox_preview.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: Universal Containers (UC) is embarked on an enterprise Salesforce transformation journey. UC would like to streamline and automate deployment to different sandboxes during the build phase. Upon customer acceptance in UAT, the company also requested to automate the production deployment. As the deployment architect, what is the recommendation to satisfy the customer requirements?
optionA: Recommend using a Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment tool and build the pipeline to deploy to sandboxes and production.
optionB: Recommend using SFDX and document the deployment commands with steps to be executed for each environment.
optionC: Recommend using the ANT script and build a custom application to run the script and use change sets to deploy supported metadata.
optionD: Recommend using an AppExchange solution that packages deployment components and run the deployment wizard to track results.
explanation:
A CI/CD tool (Jenkins, GitHub Actions, Azure DevOps, etc.) with a fully automated pipeline is the correct recommendation for streamlined, automated deployments across all environments — from dev sandboxes through to production. It automates builds, tests, and deployments with full visibility and auditability. SFDX with documented manual steps (B) still requires manual intervention. An ANT script with change sets (C) mixes tools and adds complexity. An AppExchange deployment wizard (D) is not a standard CI/CD pipeline and may not support all metadata types.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/salesforce-cli-reference/guide/cli_reference_project_deploy_start.html

question: Universal Containers has a full sandbox that will be used to analyze and fix bugs found in production. Which two items should the architect recommend to ensure that bugs found in production are more easily analyzed in this full sandbox? Choose 2 answers
optionA: Refresh the full sandbox after every deployment in production.
optionB: Create a daily process of copying new and changed data in production to the full sandbox.
optionC: Before any deployment in production, the same process must be performed in this sandbox first.
optionD: Perform a Refresh Data in the full sandbox.
explanation:
A Full sandbox can be refreshed only once every 29 days, so aligning it with production after every deployment is not something the platform allows - which rules out the refresh-driven option and forces the two that work. Copying new and changed records from production on a daily schedule keeps the data current between refreshes, so a bug reported this morning can be reproduced against records that resemble this morning's. Running every deployment through the sandbox first keeps its metadata in step with production, so a defect reproduced there is a defect in the code rather than an artefact of drift.
The remaining option describes an action that does not exist. Salesforce documents one refresh mechanism, which "updates its metadata from the source org" and, for a clone or a template-based sandbox, "updates the org's data and its metadata". What you can choose is which data a refresh copies, not whether to refresh data on its own.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.data_sandbox_refresh.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.create_test_instance.htm&language=en_US&type=5

corrected.note: Answer stands. The old explanation claimed a Refresh Data action exists and is "only available for Partial Copy and Developer Pro sandboxes". There is no such action: Salesforce documents a single refresh that updates metadata, and data too for clones and template-based sandboxes.

question: Universal Containers (UC) has developed extensions of Salesforce Service Cloud using the change set development model. Recently, UC acquired a company whose development team uses the org development model. The UC CTO wants both teams to work on a single org and follow the same set of processes. Which development model should the architect recommend for the consolidated development team?
optionA: Org development model, because the acquired company's team is already using it and it is better than the change set development model.
optionB: Package development model, because it allows packages to be created and deployed using declarative tools without writing code.
optionC: Package development model, so teams can build release artifacts that can be tested and released independently from artifacts for other projects.
optionD: Change set development model, because UC is already using it, so it will face less resistance.
explanation:
Two teams merging into one org need a model where each can release without waiting on the other, and that is what package development provides: work is organized into versioned packages built from source, so each team ships an artefact that is tested and installed on its own schedule. Scratch orgs give every feature branch a reproducible environment, and continuous integration falls out of the same source-driven arrangement.
The alternatives all pick a winner rather than solving the problem. Standardizing on either team's current model settles an argument about habit, not about how two streams share one org, and change sets in particular give no versioning and no independent release path. The one remaining option misdescribes the package model - it is CLI and source driven, not a declarative point-and-click alternative.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_unlocked_pkg_intro.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_scratch_orgs.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.sfdx_dev.meta/sfdx_dev/sfdx_dev_ci.htm

question: Universal Containers (UC) has developed a managed package targeted for AppExchange. The product includes Apex code to customize and create layouts. UC is in the testing phase and the package is not yet certified. During testing on the target org, the Apex code for the layouts fails. Why are the Apex classes not able to access the metadata of the target org during testing?
optionA: Apex Settings to allow access to metadata is not switched on.
optionB: UC needs to turn on Apex Settings within the custom metadata type.
optionC: The solution is flawed. UC should utilize the Tooling API from a web service call to modify the layouts.
optionD: UC needs to get the managed package certified by the Salesforce security review.
explanation:
Salesforce gates Apex metadata access on package certification, but it provides a switch for exactly the situation this question describes - a package still in testing. The rule is stated plainly: Apex classes in a package that has not passed security review "can't access public or protected metadata unless the Deploy Metadata from Non-Certified Package Versions via Apex org preference is enabled". That preference lives in Setup under Apex Settings and has to be turned on in the target org by an administrator.
So the failure is a missing org preference in the org being tested against, not a missing certification. Certification would also lift the restriction, but waiting for security review before you can test the package is the wrong way round, and the preference exists so that uncertified packages can be exercised in a real org first.
The remaining options misplace the setting or the mechanism: it is an org preference under Apex Settings, not something configured on a custom metadata type, and switching to the Tooling API does not avoid the restriction, which is about what packaged Apex may do in a subscriber org rather than which API it calls.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_metadata_security.htm
https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/atlas.en-us.apexcode.meta/apexcode/apex_metadata.htm

corrected.note: Answer moved D to A. The Apex Developer Guide documents the exact control: Apex in a non-security-reviewed package cannot reach subscriber metadata unless the "Deploy Metadata from Non-Certified Package Versions via Apex" org preference is enabled, in Setup under Apex Settings. The old explanation asserted that no such Apex Settings toggle exists and that certification was the only route.

question: Universal Containers has multiple projects being developed in parallel. One project is in the testing phase and the testing team found a list of issues on items that will be deployed to production. As the project deadline is short, the customer team proposes that the fixes be done in the test sandbox and then deployed to production. What should the Architect recommend?
optionA: Recommend the customer team's proposal to fix the issues in the testing environment and deploy them to production.
optionB: Recommend fixing the issues in the development environment and deploying the changes directly to production.
optionC: Recommend fixing the issues in the development sandbox, migrating them to testing, and deploying to production after testing.
optionD: Recommend fixing the issues in the test environment and migrating the changes to the development sandbox.
explanation:
Fixing in the test sandbox and shipping from there breaks the direction the pipeline depends on. Changes flow one way - development, then test, then production - and a fix that enters halfway leaves the development sandbox without it. The next release from development then overwrites the fix in production, and the defect returns with an authoritative-looking deployment behind it. That is the failure mode the deadline pressure is hiding.
So the fix belongs in the development sandbox, migrates into the test environment where the same team that found the issue verifies it, and reaches production through the route every other change takes. Back-porting from test to development afterwards reverses the flow and depends on someone remembering to do it, and deploying from development straight to production skips the verification step that produced the list of issues in the first place.
References:
https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/org-development-model/plan-for-changes-to-your-org2
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/2014/12/salesforce1-enterprise-environment-management

question: Universal Containers has just initiated a project to implement a partner community. The application will be deployed into a production environment currently in use by a large Salesforce user base. The project manager has insisted that the development and testing team use a single developer sandbox. What is the risk with this approach?
optionA: Testers will encounter platform limits due to developer sandbox capacity limits.
optionB: Testers will experience functional changes throughout testing due to not having isolation from development.
optionC: Testers will hit governor limits due to large volume of users in the developer sandbox.
optionD: Refreshing the developer sandbox will take significant time.
explanation:
When developers and testers share a single sandbox, developers continue committing code changes while testers are executing test cases. This means the application behavior changes mid-cycle underneath the test cases, causing testers to observe unexpected results unrelated to actual defects. The root cause is lack of environment isolation. Platform limits (A) and governor limits (C) are not specific to a shared sandbox. Refresh time (D) is a management concern, not the primary risk of sharing environments.
References:
https://developer.salesforce.com/blogs/2014/12/salesforce1-enterprise-environment-management
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.create_test_instance.htm&language=en_US&type=5

question: A release will be deployed over a weekend, one week after Salesforce updates the production environment (e.g., from Winter to Spring). UC has found that a full sandbox refresh can take several days. What should the architect suggest as an optimal deployment plan?
optionA: Two weeks before go-live, deploy to Staging and then refresh the Staging and Production support sandboxes. Deploy from Staging to Production at go-live.
optionB: Approximately six weeks before go-live, ensure the sandbox will be on the release preview. One week before go-live, deploy to Staging. Deploy from Staging to Production at go-live.
optionC: One month before go-live, deploy to Staging and to Production Support. Deploy from Production Support to Production at go-live.
optionD: One week before go-live, initiate the Staging sandbox refresh and then immediately deploy to Staging. Deploy from Staging to Production at go-live.
explanation:
Production takes the new release a week before go-live, so the staging environment has to be on that release when the final rehearsal runs - otherwise the deployment is proven against a platform version production is no longer on. The lever for that is the preview window, which sits roughly a month or more ahead of the earliest production upgrade: a sandbox created or refreshed inside it is placed on a preview instance and receives the release early. Making that arrangement about six weeks out, then deploying to Staging a week before go-live, gives a rehearsal on the same version production will be running.
The alternatives fail on timing. A refresh started a week out can run for days on a Full sandbox with no guarantee of finishing, and a refresh two weeks out risks falling outside the preview window and landing on the old release - after which the 29-day interval blocks a second attempt.
References:
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.data_sandbox_preview.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=platform.data_sandbox_refresh.htm&language=en_US&type=5
https://help.salesforce.com/s/articleView?id=000380490&language=en_US&type=1
